Millions of people in the U.S. are affected by mental illness each year. It’s important to measure how common mental illness is, so we can understand its physical, social and financial impact — and so we can show that no one is alone. These numbers are also powerful tools for raising public awareness, stigma-busting and advocating for better health care.

Mental Health by the Numbers is based on the most current and representative sources available, according to NAMI. Data is from the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), Centers for Disease Control (CDC), National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) and others. Infographics include statistics that NAMI believes will be most useful to a general audience. Infographic sources, as well as sources for additional statistics, are included in hyperlinks below.

## Fast Facts

### 1 in 5

More than 1 in 5 U.S. adults experience mental illness each year

[Source](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56287/2024-nsduh-annual-national-report.pdf)

### 1 in 20

More than 1 in 20 U.S. adults experience serious mental illness each year

[Source](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56287/2024-nsduh-annual-national-report.pdf)

### 1 in 7

More than 1 in 7 U.S. youth ages 6-17 experience a mental health disorder each year

[Source](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapediatrics/fullarticle/2724377?guestAccessKey=f689aa19-31f1-481d-878a-6bf83844536a)

### 50%

of all lifetime mental illness begins by age 14, and 75% by age 24

[Source](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15939837)

### 2nd leading

Suicide is the 2nd leading cause of death among people ages 10-24

## The Ripple Effect Of Mental Illness

* * *

![Image 5](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/NAMI_Ripple_2023_Header.jpg)

[Download Infographic](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/NAMI_Impact_RippleEffect_2025.pdf)

Having a mental illness can make it challenging to live everyday life and maintain recovery. Beyond the individual, these challenges ripple out through our families, our communities, and our world.

### Person

*   Risk of cardiometabolic disease is up to[**2x**](https://www.research.unipd.it/bitstream/11577/3383700/2/firth2019.pdf)higher in people with mental illness compared to people without mental illness
*   People with depression have a[**40%**](https://www.research.unipd.it/bitstream/11577/3383700/2/firth2019.pdf)higher risk of developing cardiac disease, hypertension, stroke, diabetes, metabolic syndrome, or obesity than the general population
*   [**34.5%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.17a)of U.S. adults with mental illness also have a substance use disorder
*   [**6.9%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.7a)of U.S. adults with mental illness are unemployed compared to 4.3% of U.S. adults without mental illness
*   High school students with recent symptoms of depression are more than[2x](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29195763)as likely to drop out compared to their peers
*   Students ages 6-17 with mental, emotional or behavioral problems are more than[2x](https://www.childhealthdata.org/browse/survey/results?q=11602&r=1&g=1216)as likely to repeat a grade

### Family

*   At least[8.4 million](https://www.caregiving.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/NAC_Mental_Illness_Study_2016_FINAL_WEB.pdf)people in the U.S. provide care to an adult with a mental or emotional health issue
*   Caregivers of adults with mental or emotional health issues spend an average of[32 hours](https://www.caregiving.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/NAC_Mental_Illness_Study_2016_FINAL_WEB.pdf)per week providing unpaid care

### Community

*   In 2024,[**18.1%**](https://files.hudexchange.info/reports/published/CoC_PopSub_NatlTerrDC_2024.pdf)of people experiencing homelessness in the U.S had a serious mental illness
*   [**12.3%**](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nhsr/nhsr181.pdf)of emergency department visits made by U.S. adults each year are related to mental health
*   Mental health and substance use conditions led to more than[**1.65 million**](https://datatools.ahrq.gov/hcup-fast-stats/)inpatient hospitalizations in the U.S. in 2022
*   Among people in the U.S. under age 18, depressive disorders are the[**#2**](https://datatools.ahrq.gov/hcup-fast-stats/)cause of inpatient hospitalizations after excluding those related to pregnancy and birth
*   [**17.6%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt53159/2023-nsduh-pop-slides-veterans.pdf)of U.S. Veterans experienced a mental illness in 2023 (3.5 million people)
*   [9.6%](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/DOD-Health-of-the-Force-2021.pdf)of Active Component service members in the U.S. military experienced a mental health or substance use condition in 2021
*   Across the U.S. economy, serious mental illness causes[$193.2 billion](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18463104)in lost earnings each year
*   Schizophrenia led to an excess economic burden of[**$343.2 billion**](https://www.psychiatrist.com/jcp/economic-burden-schizophrenia-united-states/)in the U.S. in 2019

### World

*   Depression and anxiety disorders cost the global economy[$1 trillion](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lanpsy/article/PIIS2215-0366(16)30024-4/fulltext)in lost productivity each year
*   Globally, mental health disorders are the[**leading cause**](https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/356119/9789240049338-eng.pdf?sequence=1)of years lived with disability

Reviewed and updated 2025

## It’s Okay To Talk About Suicide

* * *

![Image 7](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/NAMI_Suicide_2025_banner.png)

[Download Infographic](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/NAMI_Suicide_2025.pdf)

Thoughts of suicide can be frightening. But by reaching out for help or checking in with family and friends, we can avoid devastating outcomes.

*   More than 1 in 20 U.S. adults ([5.5%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56287/2024-nsduh-annual-national-report.pdf)) have serious thoughts of suicide each year. 
*   Suicide was the[10th leading](https://wisqars.cdc.gov/lcd/?o=LCD&y1=2024&y2=2024&ct=11&cc=ALL&g=00&s=0&r=0&ry=3&e=0&ar=lcd1age&at=groups&ag=lcd1age&a1=0&a2=199)cause of death overall in the U.S. in 2024.
*   Suicide was the[**2nd leading**](https://wisqars.cdc.gov/lcd/?o=LCD&y1=2024&y2=2024&ct=11&cc=ALL&g=00&s=0&r=0&ry=3&e=0&ar=lcd1age&at=groups&ag=lcd1age&a1=0&a2=199)cause of death among people ages 10-14 and among people ages 15-24 in the U.S. in 2024.
*   In 2022, nearly 49,000 lives were lost to suicide in the U.S. — about 1 death every[**11 minutes**](https://www.cdc.gov/injury/priorities/index.html).
*   [46%](https://archive.cdc.gov/#/details?url=https://www.cdc.gov/vitalsigns/suicide/index.html)of people who die by suicide had a diagnosed mental health condition
*   [90%](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11728849/)of people who die by suicide may have experienced symptoms of a mental health disorder, according to interviews with family, friends and medical professionals (also known as psychological autopsy)
*   Annual prevalence of serious thoughts of suicide among U.S. adults, by demographic group: 
    *   Non-Hispanic Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander:[**2.6%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.71b)
    *   Non-Hispanic Asian:[**4.4%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.71b)
    *   Non-Hispanic White:[**5.4%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.71b)
    *   Hispanic or Latino:[**5.4%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.71b)
    *   Non-Hispanic Black:**[5.5%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.71b)**
    *   Non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native:[**7.3%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.71b)
    *   Non-Hispanic Multiracial:[**10.7%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.71b)
    *   Male:†[**5.5%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.71b)
    *   Female:†[**5.5%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.71b)
    *   Lesbian, Gay or Bisexual:[**18.0%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt53159/2023-nsduh-pop-slides-lbgplus.pdf)

*   [79%](https://wisqars.cdc.gov/nvdrs/?rt=3&rt2=0&y=2022&g=00&i=1&m=20810&s=0&r=0&e=0&rl=0&pc=0&pr=0&h=0&ml=0&a=ALL&a1=0&a2=199&g1=0&g2=199&r1=NVDRS-INTENT&r2=NONE&r3=NONE&r4=NONE)of people who die by suicide in the U.S. are male‡
*   The suicide rate is nearly[**4x**](https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/statistics/suicide)higher among males‡ than females‡ in the U.S.
*   Transgender adults are[nearly 9x](https://transequality.org/sites/default/files/docs/usts/USTS-Full-Report-Dec17.pdf)more likely to attempt suicide at some point in their lifetime compared to the general population

### You Are Not Alone

*   **[16.5%](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapediatrics/fullarticle/2724377?guestAccessKey=f689aa19-31f1-481d-878a-6bf83844536a)**of U.S. youth ages 6-17 experienced a mental health disorder in 2016 (7.7 million people)
*   **[40%](https://www.cdc.gov/yrbs/dstr/pdf/YRBS-2023-Data-Summary-Trend-Report.pdf)**of U.S. high school students experienced persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness in 2023
*   **[65%](https://www.cdc.gov/yrbs/dstr/pdf/YRBS-2023-Data-Summary-Trend-Report.pdf)**of U.S. LGBTQ+ high school students experienced persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness in 2023
*   In 2023,**[29%](https://www.cdc.gov/yrbs/dstr/pdf/YRBS-2023-Data-Summary-Trend-Report.pdf)**of U.S. high school students experienced poor mental health in the past 30 days
*   In 2023,**[53%](https://www.cdc.gov/yrbs/dstr/pdf/YRBS-2023-Data-Summary-Trend-Report.pdf)**of U.S. LGBTQ+ high school students experienced poor mental health in the past 30 days
*   **[32.2%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56287/2024-nsduh-annual-national-report.pdf)**of U.S. young adults ages 18-25 experienced mental illness in 2024 (11.6 million people)
*   **[66%](https://www.thetrevorproject.org/survey-2024/#anxiety-depression)**of U.S. LGBTQ+ young people ages 13-24 reported experiencing recent symptoms of anxiety in 2023
*   **[53%](https://www.thetrevorproject.org/survey-2024/#anxiety-depression)**of U.S. LGBTQ+ young people ages 13-24 reported experiencing recent symptoms of depression in 2023

### Mental Health Care Matters

*   **[50.6%](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapediatrics/fullarticle/2724377?guestAccessKey=f689aa19-31f1-481d-878a-6bf83844536a)**of U.S. youth ages 6-17 with a mental health disorder received treatment in 2016
*   **[49.9%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56287/2024-nsduh-annual-national-report.pdf)**of U.S. young adults ages 18-25 with a mental illness received treatment in 2024

### It’s Okay to Talk About Suicide

*   Suicide is the**[2 nd leading](https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/statistics/suicide)**cause of death among people ages 10-14 and among people ages 15-24 in the U.S.
*   **[20%](https://www.cdc.gov/yrbs/dstr/pdf/YRBS-2023-Data-Summary-Trend-Report.pdf)**of U.S. high school students had serious thoughts of suicide in 2023
*   **[41%](https://www.cdc.gov/yrbs/dstr/pdf/YRBS-2023-Data-Summary-Trend-Report.pdf)**of U.S. LGBTQ+ high school students had serious thoughts of suicide in 2023
*   U.S. LGBTQ+ high school students are over**[3x](https://www.cdc.gov/yrbs/dstr/pdf/YRBS-2023-Data-Summary-Trend-Report.pdf)**more likely to attempt suicide compared to their straight, cisgender peers
*   **[39%](https://www.thetrevorproject.org/survey-2024/#suicide-risk)**of U.S. LGBTQ+ young people ages 13-24 had serious thoughts of suicide in 2023
*   **[12.6%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56287/2024-nsduh-annual-national-report.pdf)**of U.S. young adults ages 18-25 had serious thoughts of suicide in 2024

### Mental Health Belongs in School

*   More than**[two thirds](https://ies.ed.gov/schoolsurvey/spp/SPP_April_Infographic_Mental_Health_and_Well_Being.pdf)**of U.S. public schools report an increase in students seeking mental health services at school since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic
*   Only**[56%](https://ies.ed.gov/schoolsurvey/spp/SPP_April_Infographic_Mental_Health_and_Well_Being.pdf)**of U.S. public schools say they can effectively provide mental health services to all students in need

## 2020: Recognizing The Impact

* * *

![Image 9](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/NAMI_2020MH_ByTheNumbers_Adults-th-734.png)

[Download Infographic](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/NAMI_2020MH_ByTheNumbers_Adults-r.pdf)

2020 was a year of challenges, marked by loss and the uncertainty of the COVID-19 pandemic.

We must recognize the significant impact of the pandemic on our mental health—and the importance of increasing access to timely and effective care for those who need it.

*   [1 in 15](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)U.S adults experienced both a substance use disorder and mental illness
*   [12+ million](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)U.S adults had serious thoughts of suicide
*   [1 in 5](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)U.S adults report that the pandemic had a significant negative impact on their mental health 
    *   [45%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)of those with mental illness
    *   [55%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)of those with serious mental illness

*   Among people aged 12 and older who drink alcohol,[15%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)report increased drinking
*   Among people aged 12 and older who use drugs,[10%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)report increased use
*   Among U.S. adults who received mental health services: 
    *   [17.7 million](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)experienced delays or cancellations in appointments
    *   [7.3 million](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)experienced delays in getting prescriptions
    *   [4.9 million](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)were unable to access needed care

*   [26.3 million](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)U.S adults received virtual mental health services in the past year 
    *   [34%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)of those with mental illness
    *   [50%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)of those with serious mental illness

Youth and young adults experienced a unique set of challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic—isolation from peers, adapting to virtual learning, and changes to sleep habits and other routines.

We must recognize the significant impact of these experiences on young people’s mental health—and the importance of providing the education, care and support they need.

*   Among U.S. adolescents (aged 12-17): 
    *   [1 in 6](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)experienced a major depressive episode (MDE)
    *   [3 million](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)had serious thoughts of suicide
    *   [31% increase](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/wr/mm7024e1.htm)in mental health-related emergency department visits

*   Among U.S. young adults (aged 18-25): 
    *   [1 in 3](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)experienced a mental illness
    *   [1 in 10](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)experienced a serious mental illness
    *   [3.8 million](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)had serious thoughts of suicide

*   [1 in 5](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)young people report that the pandemic had a significant negative impact on their mental health 
    *   [18%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)of adolescents
    *   [23%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/report/2020-nsduh-detailed-tables)of young adults
    *   [Nearly ½](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/report/2020-nsduh-detailed-tables)of young people with mental health concerns report a significant negative impact

*   [1 in 10](https://aspe.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/documents/0bcc372f4755cca29ebc80a47cfe300e/child-adolescent-mh-covid.pdf)people under age 18 experience a mental health condition following a COVID-19 diagnosis
*   Increased use of alcohol among those who drink: 
    *   [15%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)of adolescents
    *   [18%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)of young adults

*   Increased use of drugs among those who use: 
    *   [15%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)of adolescents
    *   [19%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt35325/NSDUHFFRPDFWHTMLFiles2020/2020NSDUHFFR1PDFW102121.pdf)of young adults

## Mental Illness And The Criminal Justice System

* * *

![Image 11](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/NAMI_CriminalJusticeSystem-th-734.png)

[Download Infographic](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/NAMI_CriminalJusticeSystem-v5.pdf)

People with mental illness deserve help, not handcuffs. Yet people with mental illness are overrepresented in our nation’s jails and prisons. We need to reduce criminal justice system involvement and increase investments in mental health care.

### Criminal Justice System

*   About[2 million times](https://ps.psychiatryonline.org/doi/full/10.1176/ps.2009.60.6.761)each year, people with serious mental illness are booked into jails.
*   About 2 in 5 people who are incarcerated have a history of mental illness ([37%](https://www.bjs.gov/content/pub/pdf/imhprpji1112.pdf)in state and federal prisons and[44%](https://www.bjs.gov/content/pub/pdf/imhprpji1112.pdf)held in local jails).
*   [66%](https://www.bjs.gov/content/pub/pdf/imhprpji1112.pdf)of women in prison reported having a history of mental illness, almost twice the percentage of men in prison.
*   Nearly[one in four](https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/investigations/police-shootings-database/)people shot and killed by police officers between 2015 and 2020 had a mental health condition.
*   Suicide is the[leading cause](https://www.bjs.gov/content/pub/pdf/mlj0014_sum.pdf)of death for people held in local jails.
*   An estimated[4,000](https://law.yale.edu/sites/default/files/documents/pdf/Liman/asca_liman_2018_restrictive_housing_revised_sept_25_2018_-_embargoed_unt.pdf)people with serious mental illness are held in solitary confinement inside U.S. prisons.

### Communities

*   [70%](https://nyjn.org/snapshot-from-njjn-2021-policy-platform-keeping-children-with-mental-health-challenges-out-of-the-youth-legal-system/)of youth in the juvenile justice system have a diagnosable mental health condition.
*   Youth in detention are[10 times](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18664994/)more likely to suffer from psychosis than youth in the community.
*   About[50,000](https://bjs.ojp.gov/content/pub/pdf/vpj1112.pdf)veterans are held in local jails —[55%](https://bjs.ojp.gov/content/pub/pdf/vpj1112.pdf)report experiencing a mental illness.
*   Among incarcerated people with a mental health condition, non-white individuals are[more likely](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4539829/)to go to solitary confinement, be injured, and stay longer in jail.

### Access to Care

*   About 3 in 5 people ([63%](https://bjs.ojp.gov/content/pub/pdf/imhprpji1112.pdf)) with a history of mental illness do not receive mental health treatment while incarcerated in state and federal prisons.
*   Less than half of people ([45%](https://bjs.ojp.gov/content/pub/pdf/imhprpji1112.pdf)) with a history of mental illness receive mental health treatment while held in local jails.
*   People who have healthcare coverage upon release from incarceration are[more likely](https://files.csgjusticecenter.org/critical-connections/Critical-Connections-Full-Report.pdf)to engage in services that reduce recidivism.

## Mental Health & Access To Care In Rural America

* * *

![Image 12](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/NAMI_MHinRuralAmerica-th-734.png)

[Download Infographic](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/NAMI_MHinRuralAmerica.pdf)

People from all communities are affected by mental illness, but rural Americans often experience unique barriers to managing their mental health.

*   Among U.S. adults in nonmetropolitan areas, 2020: 
    *   [21%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/report/2020-nsduh-detailed-tables)experienced mental illness
    *   [6%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/report/2020-nsduh-detailed-tables)experienced serious mental illness
    *   [13%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/report/2020-nsduh-detailed-tables)experienced a substance use disorder
    *   [5%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/report/2020-nsduh-detailed-tables)had serious thoughts of suicide

### Access to Treatment is Severely Limited

*   Among U.S adults in nonmetropolitan areas, 2020: 
    *   [48%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/report/2020-nsduh-detailed-tables)with a mental illness received treatment
    *   [62%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/report/2020-nsduh-detailed-tables)with a serious mental illness received treatment

*   Compared to suburban and urban residents, rural Americans: 
    *   Must travel[2x](https://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2018/12/12/how-far-americans-live-from-the-closest-hospital-differs-by-community-type/)as far to their nearest hospital
    *   Are[2x](https://www.americanprogress.org/issues/economy/news/2021/07/12/501530/rural-broadband-investments-promote-inclusive-economy/)as likely to lack broadband internet, limiting access to telehealth

*   [25+ Million](https://data.hrsa.gov/default/generatehpsaquarterlyreport)rural Americans live in a Mental Health Professional Shortage Area, where there are too few providers to meet demand

### Some Populations Face Additional Challenges

*   [53%](https://www.fb.org/files/Impacts_of_COVID-19_on_Rural_Mental_Health_1.6.21.pdf)of rural adults say the COVID-19 pandemic has affected their mental health 
    *   66% of farmers and farmworkers
    *   71% of younger adults aged 18-34

*   [Many rural states](https://www.cdc.gov/prams/php/data-research/mch-indicators-by-site.html)have a postpartum depression rate higher than the national average of 13%: 
    *   21% in Alabama
    *   22% in Mississippi
    *   23% in Arkansas

*   Rural youth are at an increased risk of suicide, but highly rural areas have[fewer youth suicide prevention services](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7582123/)

Millions of people in the U.S. are affected by mental illness each year. It’s important to measure how common mental illness is, so we can understand its physical, social and financial impact — and so we can show that no one is alone. These numbers are also powerful tools for raising public awareness, stigma-busting and advocating for better health care.

Mental Health by the Numbers is based on the most current and representative sources available, according to NAMI. Data is from the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), Centers for Disease Control (CDC), National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) and others. Infographics include statistics that NAMI believes will be most useful to a general audience. Infographic sources, as well as sources for additional statistics, are included in hyperlinks below.

## Fast Facts

### 1 in 5

More than 1 in 5 U.S. adults experience mental illness each year

[Source](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56287/2024-nsduh-annual-national-report.pdf)

### 1 in 20

More than 1 in 20 U.S. adults experience serious mental illness each year

[Source](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56287/2024-nsduh-annual-national-report.pdf)

### 1 in 7

More than 1 in 7 U.S. youth ages 6-17 experience a mental health disorder each year

[Source](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapediatrics/fullarticle/2724377?guestAccessKey=f689aa19-31f1-481d-878a-6bf83844536a)

### 50%

of all lifetime mental illness begins by age 14, and 75% by age 24

[Source](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15939837)

### 2nd leading

Suicide is the 2nd leading cause of death among people ages 10-24

[Source](https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/statistics/suicide)

## You Are Not Alone

![Image 3](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/NAMI_YouAreNotAlone_2025_banner.png)

Millions of people are affected by mental illness each year. Across the country, many people just like you work, perform, create, compete, laugh, love and inspire every day.

*   [23.4%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56287/2024-nsduh-annual-national-report.pdf)of U.S. adults experienced mental illness in 2024 (61.5 million people). This represents more than 1 in 5 adults.
*   [5.6%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56287/2024-nsduh-annual-national-report.pdf)of U.S. adults experienced serious mental illness in 2024 (14.6 million people). This represents 1 in 20 adults.
*   [16.5%](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapediatrics/fullarticle/2724377?guestAccessKey=f689aa19-31f1-481d-878a-6bf83844536a)of U.S. youth aged 6-17 experienced a mental health disorder in 2016 (7.7 million people). This represents more than 1 in 7 youth.

    *   Schizophrenia:[<1%](https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/statistics/schizophrenia.shtml)

## Mental Health Care Matters

* * *

![Image 4](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/NAMI_MentalHealthCareMatters_2020_th-734.png)

[Download Infographic](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/NAMI_MentalHealthCareMatterS_2025.pdf)

*   [52.1%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56287/2024-nsduh-annual-national-report.pdf)of U.S. adults with mental illness received treatment in 2024
*   [70.8%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56287/2024-nsduh-annual-national-report.pdf)of U.S. adults with serious mental illness received treatment in 2024
*   [50.6%](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapediatrics/fullarticle/2724377?guestAccessKey=f689aa19-31f1-481d-878a-6bf83844536a)of U.S. youth aged 6-17 with a mental health disorder received treatment in 2016
*   The average delay between onset of mental illness symptoms and treatment is[11 years](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1361014/)
*   Annual treatment rates among U.S. adults with mental illness, by demographic group:* 
    *   Non-Hispanic Asian:[**32.5%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.21b)
    *   Non-Hispanic Black or African American:[**38.5%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.21b)
    *   Hispanic or Latino:[**44.1%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.21b)

## The Ripple Effect Of Mental Illness

* * *

![Image 5](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/NAMI_Ripple_2023_Header.jpg)

[Download Infographic](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/NAMI_Impact_RippleEffect_2025.pdf)

Having a mental illness can make it challenging to live everyday life and maintain recovery. Beyond the individual, these challenges ripple out through our families, our communities, and our world.

### Person

*   Risk of cardiometabolic disease is up to[**2x**](https://www.research.unipd.it/bitstream/11577/3383700/2/firth2019.pdf)higher in people with mental illness compared to people without mental illness
*   People with depression have a[**40%**](https://www.research.unipd.it/bitstream/11577/3383700/2/firth2019.pdf)higher risk of developing cardiac disease, hypertension, stroke, diabetes, metabolic syndrome, or obesity than the general population
*   [**34.5%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.17a)of U.S. adults with mental illness also have a substance use disorder
*   [**6.9%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.7a)of U.S. adults with mental illness are unemployed compared to 4.3% of U.S. adults without mental illness
*   High school students with recent symptoms of depression are more than[2x](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29195763)as likely to drop out compared to their peers
*   Students ages 6-17 with mental, emotional or behavioral problems are more than[2x](https://www.childhealthdata.org/browse/survey/results?q=11602&r=1&g=1216)as likely to repeat a grade

### Family

*   At least[8.4 million](https://www.caregiving.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/NAC_Mental_Illness_Study_2016_FINAL_WEB.pdf)people in the U.S. provide care to an adult with a mental or emotional health issue
*   Caregivers of adults with mental or emotional health issues spend an average of[32 hours](https://www.caregiving.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/NAC_Mental_Illness_Study_2016_FINAL_WEB.pdf)per week providing unpaid care

### Community

*   In 2024,[**18.1%**](https://files.hudexchange.info/reports/published/CoC_PopSub_NatlTerrDC_2024.pdf)of people experiencing homelessness in the U.S had a serious mental illness
*   [**12.3%**](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nhsr/nhsr181.pdf)of emergency department visits made by U.S. adults each year are related to mental health
*   Mental health and substance use conditions led to more than[**1.65 million**](https://datatools.ahrq.gov/hcup-fast-stats/)inpatient hospitalizations in the U.S. in 2022
*   Among people in the U.S. under age 18, depressive disorders are the[**#2**](https://datatools.ahrq.gov/hcup-fast-stats/)cause of inpatient hospitalizations after excluding those related to pregnancy and birth
*   [**17.6%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt53159/2023-nsduh-pop-slides-veterans.pdf)of U.S. Veterans experienced a mental illness in 2023 (3.5 million people)
*   [9.6%](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/DOD-Health-of-the-Force-2021.pdf)of Active Component service members in the U.S. military experienced a mental health or substance use condition in 2021
*   Across the U.S. economy, serious mental illness causes[$193.2 billion](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18463104)in lost earnings each year
*   Schizophrenia led to an excess economic burden of[**$343.2 billion**](https://www.psychiatrist.com/jcp/economic-burden-schizophrenia-united-states/)in the U.S. in 2019

### World

*   Depression and anxiety disorders cost the global economy[$1 trillion](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lanpsy/article/PIIS2215-0366(16)30024-4/fulltext)in lost productivity each year
*   Globally, mental health disorders are the[**leading cause**](https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/356119/9789240049338-eng.pdf?sequence=1)of years lived with disability

Reviewed and updated 2025

## It’s Okay To Talk About Suicide

* * *

![Image 7](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/NAMI_Suicide_2025_banner.png)

[Download Infographic](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/NAMI_Suicide_2025.pdf)

Thoughts of suicide can be frightening. But by reaching out for help or checking in with family and friends, we can avoid devastating outcomes.

*   More than 1 in 20 U.S. adults ([5.5%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56287/2024-nsduh-annual-national-report.pdf)) have serious thoughts of suicide each year. 
*   Suicide was the[10th leading](https://wisqars.cdc.gov/lcd/?o=LCD&y1=2024&y2=2024&ct=11&cc=ALL&g=00&s=0&r=0&ry=3&e=0&ar=lcd1age&at=groups&ag=lcd1age&a1=0&a2=199)cause of death overall in the U.S. in 2024.
*   Suicide was the[**2nd leading**](https://wisqars.cdc.gov/lcd/?o=LCD&y1=2024&y2=2024&ct=11&cc=ALL&g=00&s=0&r=0&ry=3&e=0&ar=lcd1age&at=groups&ag=lcd1age&a1=0&a2=199)cause of death among people ages 10-14 and among people ages 15-24 in the U.S. in 2024.
*   In 2022, nearly 49,000 lives were lost to suicide in the U.S. — about 1 death every[**11 minutes**](https://www.cdc.gov/injury/priorities/index.html).
*   [46%](https://archive.cdc.gov/#/details?url=https://www.cdc.gov/vitalsigns/suicide/index.html)of people who die by suicide had a diagnosed mental health condition
*   [90%](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11728849/)of people who die by suicide may have experienced symptoms of a mental health disorder, according to interviews with family, friends and medical professionals (also known as psychological autopsy)
*   Annual prevalence of serious thoughts of suicide among U.S. adults, by demographic group: 
    *   Non-Hispanic Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander:[**2.6%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.71b)
    *   Non-Hispanic Asian:[**4.4%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.71b)
    *   Non-Hispanic White:[**5.4%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.71b)
    *   Hispanic or Latino:[**5.4%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.71b)
    *   Non-Hispanic Black:**[5.5%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.71b)**
    *   Non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native:[**7.3%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.71b)
    *   Non-Hispanic Multiracial:[**10.7%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.71b)
    *   Male:†[**5.5%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.71b)
    *   Female:†[**5.5%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt56484/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/NSDUHDetailedTabs2024/2024-nsduh-detailed-tables-sect6pe.htm#tab6.71b)
    *   Lesbian, Gay or Bisexual:[**18.0%**](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt53159/2023-nsduh-pop-slides-lbgplus.pdf)

*   [79%](https://wisqars.cdc.gov/nvdrs/?rt=3&rt2=0&y=2022&g=00&i=1&m=20810&s=0&r=0&e=0&rl=0&pc=0&pr=0&h=0&ml=0&a=ALL&a1=0&a2=199&g1=0&g2=199&r1=NVDRS-INTENT&r2=NONE&r3=NONE&r4=NONE)of people who die by suicide in the U.S. are male‡
*   The suicide rate is nearly[**4x**](https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/statistics/suicide)higher among males‡ than females‡ in the U.S.
*   Transgender adults are[nearly 9x](https://transequality.org/sites/default/files/docs/usts/USTS-Full-Report-Dec17.pdf)more likely to attempt suicide at some point in their lifetime compared to the general population

## Mental Illness And The Criminal Justice System

* * *

![Image 11](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/NAMI_CriminalJusticeSystem-th-734.png)

[Download Infographic](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/NAMI_CriminalJusticeSystem-v5.pdf)

People with mental illness deserve help, not handcuffs. Yet people with mental illness are overrepresented in our nation’s jails and prisons. We need to reduce criminal justice system involvement and increase investments in mental health care.

### Criminal Justice System

*   About[2 million times](https://ps.psychiatryonline.org/doi/full/10.1176/ps.2009.60.6.761)each year, people with serious mental illness are booked into jails.
*   About 2 in 5 people who are incarcerated have a history of mental illness ([37%](https://www.bjs.gov/content/pub/pdf/imhprpji1112.pdf)in state and federal prisons and[44%](https://www.bjs.gov/content/pub/pdf/imhprpji1112.pdf)held in local jails).
*   [66%](https://www.bjs.gov/content/pub/pdf/imhprpji1112.pdf)of women in prison reported having a history of mental illness, almost twice the percentage of men in prison.
*   Nearly[one in four](https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/investigations/police-shootings-database/)people shot and killed by police officers between 2015 and 2020 had a mental health condition.
*   Suicide is the[leading cause](https://www.bjs.gov/content/pub/pdf/mlj0014_sum.pdf)of death for people held in local jails.
*   An estimated[4,000](https://law.yale.edu/sites/default/files/documents/pdf/Liman/asca_liman_2018_restrictive_housing_revised_sept_25_2018_-_embargoed_unt.pdf)people with serious mental illness are held in solitary confinement inside U.S. prisons.

### Communities

*   [70%](https://nyjn.org/snapshot-from-njjn-2021-policy-platform-keeping-children-with-mental-health-challenges-out-of-the-youth-legal-system/)of youth in the juvenile justice system have a diagnosable mental health condition.
*   Youth in detention are[10 times](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18664994/)more likely to suffer from psychosis than youth in the community.
*   About[50,000](https://bjs.ojp.gov/content/pub/pdf/vpj1112.pdf)veterans are held in local jails —[55%](https://bjs.ojp.gov/content/pub/pdf/vpj1112.pdf)report experiencing a mental illness.
*   Among incarcerated people with a mental health condition, non-white individuals are[more likely](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4539829/)to go to solitary confinement, be injured, and stay longer in jail.

### Access to Care

*   About 3 in 5 people ([63%](https://bjs.ojp.gov/content/pub/pdf/imhprpji1112.pdf)) with a history of mental illness do not receive mental health treatment while incarcerated in state and federal prisons.
*   Less than half of people ([45%](https://bjs.ojp.gov/content/pub/pdf/imhprpji1112.pdf)) with a history of mental illness receive mental health treatment while held in local jails.
*   People who have healthcare coverage upon release from incarceration are[more likely](https://files.csgjusticecenter.org/critical-connections/Critical-Connections-Full-Report.pdf)to engage in services that reduce recidivism.

## Mental Health & Access To Care In Rural America

* * *

![Image 12](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/NAMI_MHinRuralAmerica-th-734.png)

[Download Infographic](https://www.nami.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/NAMI_MHinRuralAmerica.pdf)

People from all communities are affected by mental illness, but rural Americans often experience unique barriers to managing their mental health.

*   Among U.S. adults in nonmetropolitan areas, 2020: 
    *   [21%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/report/2020-nsduh-detailed-tables)experienced mental illness
    *   [6%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/report/2020-nsduh-detailed-tables)experienced serious mental illness
    *   [13%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/report/2020-nsduh-detailed-tables)experienced a substance use disorder
    *   [5%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/report/2020-nsduh-detailed-tables)had serious thoughts of suicide

### Access to Treatment is Severely Limited

*   Among U.S adults in nonmetropolitan areas, 2020: 
    *   [48%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/report/2020-nsduh-detailed-tables)with a mental illness received treatment
    *   [62%](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/report/2020-nsduh-detailed-tables)with a serious mental illness received treatment

*   Compared to suburban and urban residents, rural Americans: 
    *   Must travel[2x](https://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2018/12/12/how-far-americans-live-from-the-closest-hospital-differs-by-community-type/)as far to their nearest hospital
    *   Are[2x](https://www.americanprogress.org/issues/economy/news/2021/07/12/501530/rural-broadband-investments-promote-inclusive-economy/)as likely to lack broadband internet, limiting access to telehealth

*   [25+ Million](https://data.hrsa.gov/default/generatehpsaquarterlyreport)rural Americans live in a Mental Health Professional Shortage Area, where there are too few providers to meet demand

### Some Populations Face Additional Challenges

*   [53%](https://www.fb.org/files/Impacts_of_COVID-19_on_Rural_Mental_Health_1.6.21.pdf)of rural adults say the COVID-19 pandemic has affected their mental health 
    *   66% of farmers and farmworkers
    *   71% of younger adults aged 18-34

*   [Many rural states](https://www.cdc.gov/prams/php/data-research/mch-indicators-by-site.html)have a postpartum depression rate higher than the national average of 13%: 
    *   21% in Alabama
    *   22% in Mississippi
    *   23% in Arkansas

*   Rural youth are at an increased risk of suicide, but highly rural areas have[fewer youth suicide prevention services](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7582123/)

# Annual **Gun Law** Scorecard®

Gun violence is a crisis our leaders cannot continue to ignore. **States must act now and protect our communities.**

It’s really simple: Gun laws save lives. We run the numbers every year, and every year we come to the same conclusion—fewer people die from gun violence in states that pass commonsense gun safety laws. Yet this crisis continues to plague America. So what are your lawmakers doing about it?

## Grading the **States**

Each year, GIFFORDS experts analyze every gun law in every state—including new laws as they’re enacted. Policies are assigned point values based on how effective they are at reducing gun violence, the points are tallied to determine grades and rankings, and the grades are compared to the latest CDC gun death data. That’s how we’ve been doing this project for 15 years now, and the results have never changed: States with stronger gun laws have lower gun death rates. Yet tens of thousands of Americans continue to die every year, because some states refuse to take action.

## America's Opinion on **Gun Safety**

It’s no surprise that Americans overwhelmingly support commonsense gun safety laws. They can see the difference between states that have effective gun laws and those that take orders from gun lobby CEOs. But unfortunately, most Americans don’t live in a state governed by those who share their views on gun safety.

A strong representative democracy requires lawmakers to take the actions that their constituents want—and the data shows Americans want stronger gun laws.

[LEARN MORE](https://giffords.org/analysis/americans-want-stronger-gun-laws/)

### State Leaders Ignore America’s Support for Commonsense Gun Laws

## States **Fight Back**

Under the Trump administration, federal agencies have taken many steps to reduce or reverse gun safety measures. They’ve cut funding, stripped resources, made it easier for dangerous people to get a gun, and more. These actions have made America a more dangerous country, but we can fight back—and this fight starts in the states.

**Below are a few of the major attacks on gun safety, as well as guidance for states moving forward.**

### Community Violence Intervention

Policy & Funding![Image 14](https://files.giffords.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/PolicyFunding.svg)

Trump cut more than $800 million in public safety grants, including about $150 million from violence intervention and prevention programs, reversing years of strategic investment in evidence-informed and community-rooted responses to violence and making this work much harder to carry out and sustain.

States must allocate dedicated funding in their annual budgets to support CVI initiatives, as well as establish sustainable, long-term funding streams for CVI outside of annual budgets.

[Learn More](https://giffords.org/analysis/state-blueprints-saving-community-violence-intervention-programs/)

### Forced Reset Triggers

Guns & Hardware![Image 16](https://files.giffords.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Gun_icon.svg)

Trump effectively legalized machine guns by settling a lawsuit and allowing for the sale of forced reset triggers, which turn semiautomatic firearms into machine guns—weapons that have been banned since 1986. Across most of the country, there is now little to prevent the proliferation of these dangerous devices.

States must ban forced reset triggers and other rapid-fire devices to protect their communities from illegal machine guns.

[Learn More](https://giffords.org/analysis/the-trump-administration-legalized-machine-guns-states-must-respond/)

### Office of Gun Violence Prevention

Policy & Funding![Image 18](https://files.giffords.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/PolicyFunding.svg)

Trump shuttered the White House Office of Gun Violence Prevention, which helped coordinate federal response efforts to mass shootings and community gun violence. It also worked directly with state and local partners to address gun violence through the implementation of the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act and executive actions on gun safety.

States must create their own dedicated infrastructure to coordinate efforts on gun violence prevention across the state, like a state office of gun violence prevention.

[Learn More](https://giffords.org/lawcenter/gun-laws/policy-areas/other-laws-policies/offices-of-gun-violence-prevention/)

### Dealer Regulations

Guns & Hardware![Image 20](https://files.giffords.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Gun_icon.svg)

Trump proposed considerable cuts to ATF staff, reducing the agency’s capacity to inspect gun dealers and do its job of enforcing federal gun laws. Additionally, Trump revoked a core ATF policy that penalized gun dealers who intentionally sold guns to criminals—making it easier for gun dealers who break the law to continue to do so.

States must better regulate gun dealers by requiring them to obtain a business license and submit to appropriate oversight.

[Learn More](https://giffords.org/lawcenter/gun-laws/policy-areas/gun-sales/gun-dealers/)

### Gun Violence Research

Policy & Funding![Image 22](https://files.giffords.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/PolicyFunding.svg)

Trump cut hundreds of staff from vital programs across the CDC and the Department of Health and Human Services, including experts who maintained key data sources, oversaw the allocation of research grants and violence prevention programs, developed and maintained injury dashboards, and so much more—all of which the gun safety movement relies on to develop solutions that will help fight gun violence.

States must establish dedicated funding streams to support existing gun violence research programs or create new ones.

[Learn More](https://giffords.org/analysis/state-blueprints-treating-gun-violence-as-the-public-health-crisis-it-is/)

### Gun Silencers & Hidden Weapons

Guns & Hardware![Image 24](https://files.giffords.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Gun_icon.svg)

Trump’s bill, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, included a radical provision that eliminated the tax necessary to acquire gun silencers, short-barreled rifles, and sawed-off shotguns—which have been effectively regulated by the National Firearms Act for nearly a century. By doing so, Trump and Congress have made it easier for violent criminals to acquire these devices.

States must enact their own bans on dangerous gun silencers, short-barreled rifles, and sawed-off shotguns, which put both law enforcement and civilians at greater risk.

[Learn More](https://giffords.org/lawcenter/gun-laws/policy-areas/hardware-ammunition/silencers/)

## Gun Industry **Responsibility**

Twenty years ago, Congress passed the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act (PLCAA), which gave the gun industry unique immunity from most lawsuits and allowed reckless companies to escape accountability. Since then, gun violence has skyrocketed—and so have gun industry profits.

**But that doesn’t mean we’re helpless to fight back.** In recent years, the gun safety movement has stepped up its fight to ensure the gun industry behaves responsibly.

Organizations like GIFFORDS are partnering with survivors and leaders in state and local government to sue gun companies to hold them responsible for mass shootings, increased violence in cities, and dangerous business practices. States are also prioritizing firearm industry responsibility legislation that sets a standard these companies must abide by.

Click on an icon in the timeline for more information about our legal and legislative wins.

[Learn More](https://giffords.org/lawcenter/gun-laws/policy-areas/other-laws-policies/gun-industry-immunity/)

# Annual **Gun Law** Scorecard®

Gun violence is a crisis our leaders cannot continue to ignore. **States must act now and protect our communities.**

It’s really simple: Gun laws save lives. We run the numbers every year, and every year we come to the same conclusion—fewer people die from gun violence in states that pass commonsense gun safety laws. Yet this crisis continues to plague America. So what are your lawmakers doing about it?

## Grading the **States**

Each year, GIFFORDS experts analyze every gun law in every state—including new laws as they’re enacted. Policies are assigned point values based on how effective they are at reducing gun violence, the points are tallied to determine grades and rankings, and the grades are compared to the latest CDC gun death data. That’s how we’ve been doing this project for 15 years now, and the results have never changed: States with stronger gun laws have lower gun death rates. Yet tens of thousands of Americans continue to die every year, because some states refuse to take action.

## America's Opinion on **Gun Safety**

It’s no surprise that Americans overwhelmingly support commonsense gun safety laws. They can see the difference between states that have effective gun laws and those that take orders from gun lobby CEOs. But unfortunately, most Americans don’t live in a state governed by those who share their views on gun safety.

A strong representative democracy requires lawmakers to take the actions that their constituents want—and the data shows Americans want stronger gun laws.

[LEARN MORE](https://giffords.org/analysis/americans-want-stronger-gun-laws/)

### State Leaders Ignore America’s Support for Commonsense Gun Laws

## States **Fight Back**

Under the Trump administration, federal agencies have taken many steps to reduce or reverse gun safety measures. They’ve cut funding, stripped resources, made it easier for dangerous people to get a gun, and more. These actions have made America a more dangerous country, but we can fight back—and this fight starts in the states.

**Below are a few of the major attacks on gun safety, as well as guidance for states moving forward.**

### Community Violence Intervention

Policy & Funding![Image 14](https://files.giffords.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/PolicyFunding.svg)

Trump cut more than $800 million in public safety grants, including about $150 million from violence intervention and prevention programs, reversing years of strategic investment in evidence-informed and community-rooted responses to violence and making this work much harder to carry out and sustain.

States must allocate dedicated funding in their annual budgets to support CVI initiatives, as well as establish sustainable, long-term funding streams for CVI outside of annual budgets.

[Learn More](https://giffords.org/analysis/state-blueprints-saving-community-violence-intervention-programs/)

### Forced Reset Triggers

Guns & Hardware![Image 16](https://files.giffords.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Gun_icon.svg)

Trump effectively legalized machine guns by settling a lawsuit and allowing for the sale of forced reset triggers, which turn semiautomatic firearms into machine guns—weapons that have been banned since 1986. Across most of the country, there is now little to prevent the proliferation of these dangerous devices.

States must ban forced reset triggers and other rapid-fire devices to protect their communities from illegal machine guns.

[Learn More](https://giffords.org/analysis/the-trump-administration-legalized-machine-guns-states-must-respond/)

### Office of Gun Violence Prevention

Policy & Funding![Image 18](https://files.giffords.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/PolicyFunding.svg)

Trump shuttered the White House Office of Gun Violence Prevention, which helped coordinate federal response efforts to mass shootings and community gun violence. It also worked directly with state and local partners to address gun violence through the implementation of the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act and executive actions on gun safety.

States must create their own dedicated infrastructure to coordinate efforts on gun violence prevention across the state, like a state office of gun violence prevention.

[Learn More](https://giffords.org/lawcenter/gun-laws/policy-areas/other-laws-policies/offices-of-gun-violence-prevention/)

### Dealer Regulations

Guns & Hardware![Image 20](https://files.giffords.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Gun_icon.svg)

Trump proposed considerable cuts to ATF staff, reducing the agency’s capacity to inspect gun dealers and do its job of enforcing federal gun laws. Additionally, Trump revoked a core ATF policy that penalized gun dealers who intentionally sold guns to criminals—making it easier for gun dealers who break the law to continue to do so.

States must better regulate gun dealers by requiring them to obtain a business license and submit to appropriate oversight.

[Learn More](https://giffords.org/lawcenter/gun-laws/policy-areas/gun-sales/gun-dealers/)

### Gun Violence Research

Policy & Funding![Image 22](https://files.giffords.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/PolicyFunding.svg)

Trump cut hundreds of staff from vital programs across the CDC and the Department of Health and Human Services, including experts who maintained key data sources, oversaw the allocation of research grants and violence prevention programs, developed and maintained injury dashboards, and so much more—all of which the gun safety movement relies on to develop solutions that will help fight gun violence.

States must establish dedicated funding streams to support existing gun violence research programs or create new ones.

[Learn More](https://giffords.org/analysis/state-blueprints-treating-gun-violence-as-the-public-health-crisis-it-is/)

### Gun Silencers & Hidden Weapons

Guns & Hardware![Image 24](https://files.giffords.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Gun_icon.svg)

Trump’s bill, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, included a radical provision that eliminated the tax necessary to acquire gun silencers, short-barreled rifles, and sawed-off shotguns—which have been effectively regulated by the National Firearms Act for nearly a century. By doing so, Trump and Congress have made it easier for violent criminals to acquire these devices.

States must enact their own bans on dangerous gun silencers, short-barreled rifles, and sawed-off shotguns, which put both law enforcement and civilians at greater risk.

[Learn More](https://giffords.org/lawcenter/gun-laws/policy-areas/hardware-ammunition/silencers/)

## Gun Industry **Responsibility**

Twenty years ago, Congress passed the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act (PLCAA), which gave the gun industry unique immunity from most lawsuits and allowed reckless companies to escape accountability. Since then, gun violence has skyrocketed—and so have gun industry profits.

**But that doesn’t mean we’re helpless to fight back.** In recent years, the gun safety movement has stepped up its fight to ensure the gun industry behaves responsibly.

Organizations like GIFFORDS are partnering with survivors and leaders in state and local government to sue gun companies to hold them responsible for mass shootings, increased violence in cities, and dangerous business practices. States are also prioritizing firearm industry responsibility legislation that sets a standard these companies must abide by.

Click on an icon in the timeline for more information about our legal and legislative wins.

[Learn More](https://giffords.org/lawcenter/gun-laws/policy-areas/other-laws-policies/gun-industry-immunity/)
