# [Life is a long story](https://lifeisalongstory.com/)

Finding hope in unlikely places: A blog by the founder of Blue Dragon Children's Foundation in Vietnam.

Menu

*   [Blog](https://lifeisalongstory.com/)
*   [About](https://lifeisalongstory.com/about-me-about-this-blog/)

[![Image 1: Life is a long story](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/cropped-Life-Is-A-Long-Story.jpg)](https://lifeisalongstory.com/)

## [Dreaming beyond survival](https://lifeisalongstory.com/dreaming-beyond-survival/)

How can kids who grow up in slavery or on the streets transform into thriving adults with bright futures?

[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Flifeisalongstory.com "Facebook")[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Life%20is%20a%20long%20story%20-%20Finding%20hope%20in%20unlikely%20places%3A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20A%20blog%20by%20%20the%20founder%20of%20Blue%20Dragon%20Children%27s%20Foundation%20in%20Vietnam.&url=https%3A%2F%2Flifeisalongstory.com "Twitter")[](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https%3A%2F%2Flifeisalongstory.com "Linkedin")[](https://api.whatsapp.com/send?text=Life%20is%20a%20long%20story%20-%20Finding%20hope%20in%20unlikely%20places%3A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20A%20blog%20by%20%20the%20founder%20of%20Blue%20Dragon%20Children%27s%20Foundation%20in%20Vietnam.%20https%3A%2F%2Flifeisalongstory.com "Whatsapp")[](https://lifeisalongstory.com/ "Email")

The news from Blue Dragon last week was of both triumph and heartbreak.

After weeks of nail-biting planning and preparing, several rescue operations came to completion.

Most of the people we rescued had been enslaved in forced online scamming. These are compounds in Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos where people are forced, under threat of beatings and torture, to trick people out of their life savings using fake websites, phone messages and social media.

One of our rescues involved bringing home a 17-year-old girl from a brothel in Myanmar. She was held captive there for three years.

You can imagine the horrors she has been through.

Once each person is safe, Blue Dragon has lawyers to represent them, psychologists to provide trauma counseling and social workers to help them start over.

And while these operations were taking place, something equally transformative—but vastly different—was happening elsewhere.

### Field trip

Thirteen kids from Blue Dragon traveled to Singapore to spend the week on a cultural and educational exchange. They were accompanied by staff and some of our alumni who went to support them.

The teens visited tourist sites, stayed in wonderful accommodation (thank you, Holiday Inn Express Suites Novena!), and spent time in the homes of families who live in Singapore.

The trip was funded by United World College SEA, whose students and teachers worked for a year to raise this money.

![Image 2](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Singapore-1-1024x768.jpg)

_Blue Dragon kids in Singapore preparing their performance._

For all of the kids, this was their first time traveling abroad, staying in hotels, or even imagining a life outside Vietnam.

Seeing their awe at Singapore’s bustling streets and performing in front of an audience was a reminder of how far they’ve come—and how much potential lies within them.

Apart from having a great time, the Blue Dragon kids and the United World College students worked together to put on a grand performance at the end of the week.

### Different worlds?

Moving from life-and-death rescue operations to cultural experiences in another country might seem worlds apart.

But Blue Dragon wants kids to hope for more than mere _survival_.

When we get kids off the street, or bring them home from slavery, we want them to have the world at their feet.

To have dreams and see what’s possible beyond their own horizon.

To live a life that they love, not one that’s simply free of extreme hardship.

We’ve been fortunate to have the chance to take kids to Singapore for some years. So we’ve seen the impact that experiences like these have on young people as they grow up.

What we find is that kids who are exposed to new possibilities are much more likely to pursue an education and a career.

Some even go on to study abroad, and many end up in jobs they would never have thought possible just a few years earlier.

These different parts of our work aren’t worlds apart at all. They’re simply different points on the spectrum of ending disadvantage and transforming lives.

The 13 kids have returned to Vietnam, exhausted from an intense week and buzzing with delight.

Their eyes have been opened to something they never imagined. They’ve made new friends and performed in public.

And most importantly: They’ve shown themselves that they are more than ‘survivors’.

They were offered a chance to shine. They took the opportunity. And they succeeded.

_[Blue Dragon Child](http://www.bluedragon.org/)[r](http://www.bluedragon.org/)[en’s Foundation](http://www.bluedragon.org/)is on a mission to end human trafficking._

## [Worthless things](https://lifeisalongstory.com/worthless-things/)

Changing lives is neither a science nor an art. It takes care and commitment, sometimes over months or years. And it’s all built on one crucial but elusive foundation.

This week, I spoke on two webinars about Blue Dragon’s 20-year journey.

We started out as a handful of volunteers teaching English to street kids in Hanoi.

Today we’re working around Vietnam preventing human trafficking. We’ve led law reform initiatives, put thousands of children through school, and have rescued almost 1,700 people from slavery. So far!

During a webinar, someone asked: In our work, how do we build trust with the kids we’re helping?

An excellent question, because trust isn’t assumed. Blue Dragon’s 20 years of experience means nothing to a child we meet sleeping under a bridge, or a teenage girl locked into a brothel.

The people we meet in these crisis situations have been abused and neglected. They might not trust _anyone_, let alone a stranger from an organisation they’ve never encountered.

But we can’t help if the person doesn’t trust us. So how do we do it?

### Playing games

Back when we were starting up as a charity, we had a handful of brilliant supporters… as well as plenty of critics.

Some people assumed our work either wasn’t important or wouldn’t last long. That we’d soon discover how difficult the work was and give up.

As we continued to grow and become established, I remember one person, vastly more experienced than me, telling me that Blue Dragon’s work was useless. (To her credit, she told me this to my face).

We were doing “worthless things,” she told me. Just playing games with kids. There was no real benefit to our work.

### No strings attached

One of Blue Dragon’s key activities at that time – and still today – was weekend football for street kids.

And yes, a lot of our effort went into social activities like a drumming circle and art classes.

![Image 4](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Skye-at-drumming-1024x674.jpg)

_Skye Maconachie leading a drumming circle for street kids in 2004._  
_Today, she’s a co-CEO of the organisation._

Much of our time was spent simply getting to know kids, meeting with them, listening to them. We did all of this with no expectation or obligation.

It was up to the kids to decide whether they wanted to go back to school or continue on the streets and our care for them had no strings attached.

The purpose of all these “worthless things”? We were building trust.

Today, as we reach thousands of children and families around the country, we continue to work by the same principle.

Trust must come first and it must be earned.

Whether it’s the rescue of someone from slavery or meeting a child on the street, the decision to receive our help is theirs.

For them to make that decision, they need to know us. Not our web profile or what awards we’ve won. They need to know our character. Our heart.

### Down in the dirt

That’s why Blue Dragon staff can be found sitting by the side of the road chatting to a family. Or taking a group of kids to play games and have a meal.

![Image 5](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Street-outreach-1024x768.jpg)

_Blue Dragon street outreach workers running activities with homeless children._

It’s why our anti-trafficking initiatives in rural areas typically begin by helping communities to meet the needs that _they_ identify: a bridge to cross a stream, or a water filter system for the local school.

All of these activities meet a local need and _at the same time_ build trust with people and communities.

![Image 6](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/solar-lights-1024x458.jpg)

_Installing solar lights in a mountain village._

That trust gives us the stepping stones to then make sustainable, transformative change.

When kids know they can trust us, we can help them rebuild family connections and get back to school.

When communities see that we really do have their best interests at heart, they will work with us to keep human traffickers out of their village.

It all begins with trust.

And nothing could be more valuable.

_[Blue Dragon Child](http://www.bluedragon.org/)[r](http://www.bluedragon.org/)[en’s Foundation](http://www.bluedragon.org/)is on a mission to end human trafficking._

![Image 7](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/5872a03f1417206d1d72d3fa455decaf42f47656f4b4418313dd1d96352a9174?s=49&d=mm&r=g)Author [Michael Brosowski](https://lifeisalongstory.com/author/michael/)Posted on [November 10, 2024 November 9, 2024](https://lifeisalongstory.com/worthless-things/)[Leave a comment on Worthless things](https://lifeisalongstory.com/worthless-things/#respond)
## [Surviving the impossible](https://lifeisalongstory.com/surviving-the-impossible/)

When a simple search for work turns into a nightmare, lives are shattered in ways few can imagine. Thuy and Tuan’s stories show the brutal realities of slavery and the courage it takes to survive.

### _Thuy’s story_

When she crossed the border back to Vietnam, Thuy’s first words were: “I never thought I’d survive.”

She ventured out from home at age 28, leaving her 3-year-old son in the care of her mother and extended family.

All she wanted was the dignity of a job. To earn money for her child and parents. To have a better life.

But Thuy was tricked by people online who had gained her trust.

Instead of securing a job in a restaurant, she was trafficked to Myanmar and sold to a brothel.

The many months that she was enslaved there are a story too terrifying to tell. Trapped in a war zone, separated from her family and used as a disposable object, Thuy was sure she would die before she could ever get home.

It was almost two years before Thuy found a way to call for help. Blue Dragon organised a rescue operation and brought her home.

Even though she was free from her captors, the journey from northern Myanmar to Vietnam was frightening and tense.

Only her hope of seeing her son kept her going. And now they are back together.

![Image 8](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Thuy-and-her-son-reunited-2-768x1024.jpeg)

_Thuy and her son, reunited after almost two years apart._

### _Tuan’s story_

Tuan was deceived with similar tactics: an online connection that seemed completely authentic.

Until the moment he was overcome with force and locked into a compound.

Tuan traveled to Cambodia in search of work.

He did his research beforehand, talking to friends and scouring the internet. He believed he knew the risks and was confident no harm would come to him.

So when he realised he had been tricked and was being forced to work in captivity, his initial reaction was to demand his freedom.

Tuan was beaten and tortured into submission, then put to work in an online scamming operation. It was more than a year before he could get word to Blue Dragon, who got him out and back to his family within a few weeks.

![Image 9](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Tuan-crossing-the-border-768x1024.jpeg)

_Tuan crossing the border._

### _The chapters to come_

Even though I’ve been involved in rescue operations like these for many years, I still can’t comprehend the trauma that Thuy and Tuan are living with now.

Both put their trust in others. They went in search of employment, believing they were doing the right thing.

Their choice to leave home and travel for work was not easy and their decision was not made lightly.

So the betrayal that they experienced, and then the violence they endured month after month, left them feeling helpless and weak. And guilty.

Neither Thuy nor Tuan did anything wrong. But one of the great tricks of human traffickers is to make their victims feel like it was their own fault.

On top of the physical pain of torture and the loss of freedom, they live now with doubts about their self worth. And the question that will always haunt them: Why did this happen to them?

The toll of human trafficking is a lifetime of regret, guilt and pain.

Thuy and Tuan have a chance to start over but will need help for many months and years to come.

They were fortunate, in one sense, to be rescued: hundreds of thousands of people just like them are enslaved around Southeast Asia in brothels and scamming compounds, as they were, with no way out.

But they will carry these scars for many years to come.

## [Always more to the story](https://lifeisalongstory.com/always-more-to-the-story/)

There’s an anniversary that Bi never forgets: the day that changed his life forever. But he knows that his story is far from over.

Sipping our coffee by the lake, Bi looked over to me and said:

“November 8. It will be 6 years.”

I knew what he was referring to, because in years passed he’s mentioned this anniversary.

This is the date that, in 2018, he first encountered Blue Dragon.

It was such an important milestone in Bi’s life that he acknowledges it with every passing year.

He was still a child then. He had left his home in the village to come to the city, looking for an escape.

Life at home was hard.

His relationship with his father was fractured beyond repair. So after trying over and over, Bi eventually gave up.

Surely he could make it on the city streets alone. It couldn’t be worse than home, could it?

But it was. The streets are no place for kids to survive; not in any city, any country.

And so finding Blue Dragon was the turning point he needed.

### Fine young man

Sitting across from me now, Bi is still the same smiling, optimistic person he was when I first met him.

What’s changed is that he’s vastly more confident now. He carries himself with calm purpose; kindness beams from his smile.

Bi is in his final years of high school. Even though he’s in his early 20s, he’s enrolled in a class and is working hard at his studies. When he graduates, he plans to apply for university and earn a degree in social work.

A few nights each week, he helps out at the Blue Dragon emergency shelter. Bi works alongside staff to care for kids who we’ve just met out on the streets – kids like he once was.

![Image 11](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Bi-and-a-street-kid-927x1024.jpg)

_Bi walking with a street kid_.

But this journey of 6 years has not followed a straight line.

### The winding road

In fact, Bi’s story has had more ups and downs, more surprises along the way, than many of the young people we meet.

Over the years, there have been times when he enrolled in school… and then stopped going.

At times he’s been out sleeping rough on the streets again. For a while he returned to his village, hoping to repair his relationship with his family. When he ended up living alone in a house without electricity, he came back under the wing of Blue Dragon. And for a while he was working as a ‘shipper’, carrying goods around the city on his motorbike.

Finishing his coffee, Bi tells me that he’s not worried about the future any more. He has a plan and for the first time in his memory, he’s stable.

Above all, he’s grateful that for 6 years he’s had Blue Dragon in his life… through all the ups and downs.

And while Bi’s future is undoubtedly bright, he and I both know that there will be more to his story. More surprises, more changes along the way.

Because life is like that. It really is a long story.

And that’s OK. Bi is mature enough now to know that he doesn’t need to see the future in order to accept it.

He just needs to give it his best and to know that someone will always be there by his side.

## [It’s all in the moments](https://lifeisalongstory.com/its-all-in-the-moments/)

A girl who survives on the streets. A boy who refuses the care that he needs. What does it take to turn their lives around?

Ngoc celebrated her first birthday this week.

She turned 15.

Growing up on the streets of Ho Chi Minh City, there’s not much joy in Ngoc’s life.

Her days are about survival. That means hanging with a group of friends who can protect her and moving about the city to places she feels safe.

Ngoc has a grandmother and younger siblings. She cares for them very much. But things never seem to work out when she’s with them, so she escapes to the streets where she feels that she belongs.

Blue Dragon has been getting to know Ngoc and her friends but it takes time to build trust.

We wish we could get her back to her family right away. We wish we could heal the years of damaged relationships around her and restore the childhood that she’s lost.

And while we’d like to move fast, we know that we have to move at Ngoc’s pace.

All this will happen when she’s ready.

So day by day, we do what we can to make her life whole.

### Celebration

Friday was the first time she’s ever celebrated her own birthday.

When we learned that she had a birthday coming, we saw an opportunity to create a moment of joy.

![Image 13](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Ngocs-birthday-1024x767.jpg)

_Ngoc, 15, cutting her first birthday cake._

We bought a cake and set up in a cafe where Ngoc could invite her friends to celebrate with her.

Everyone sang happy birthday and enjoyed the sweet cake, completely forgetting the hardships of their lives.

Later, Ngoc messaged the Blue Dragon social worker to say with pride that she was so happy and had taken the remaining cake home for her siblings and her grandmother to enjoy.

I’m sure she’ll never forget that first birthday celebration.

### A crack in the armour

In Hanoi, meantime, we’ve been caring for a teen boy named Hoan.

He’s from a town 4 hours south of the city and has been on the streets for a couple of years now.

Like Ngoc, he has a family that he cares for but just can’t live with. He works at night in the tourist district of Hanoi, making enough money to get from day to day.

He enjoys meeting with Blue Dragon staff and loves going for a milk tea or a bowl of phở. But he’s wary of receiving help, guarding his independence above everything.

Two weeks ago, Hoan perforated his eardrum. It’s caused him terrible pain.

In fact, it’s been so bad that he finally accepted some help. We’ve been taking him to the hospital to treat his ear and making sure he has enough to eat while he can’t work.

His eardrum is starting to heal now. Another trip to the hospital on Saturday confirmed that he’s on the mend.

![Image 14](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Hoan-at-the-hospital-782x1024.jpg)

_Hoan at the hospital._

And after the checkup: a bowl of phở and shopping for new clothes.

Hoan beamed with joy as he chose a couple of simple t-shirts.

This tough young guy who has learned to survive on the city streets transformed into a cheerful little boy. He looked like a child on Christmas morning.

### Transformative moments

Blue Dragon’s work is about so much more than buying birthday cakes and t-shirts.

But somehow, these moments are _exactly_ what we’re about.

We all dream of changing the world. Making it a better place for those who are poor and suffering.

And much of what Blue Dragon does is focused on systemic change to end human trafficking and keep kids safe.

From day to day, though, change is incremental. Step by step.

There’s no wave of the wand, no granting of a wish to make everything better.

Instead, it starts with buying a birthday cake for a girl who’s never had one before. And taking a boy for an ear check and some shopping.

Creating those moments of joy is where change begins.

## [Massive interventions](https://lifeisalongstory.com/massive-interventions/)

Hien went to school each day and put in her best effort with a smile. But deep inside she carried fear and shame. She could see no way out.

Because it’s Blue Dragon’s 20th birthday, we’ve been looking back at kids we helped long ago and writing stories about where they are now.

This week, we shared [Hien’s story](https://www.bluedragon.org/stories/the-house-freed-her/).

We didn’t know it at the time, but Hien played an important role in shaping Blue Dragon in our early days.

### Hien’s story

I met her 20 years ago, when she was living with her mother in a truly decrepit house.

The roof had holes large enough to see the sky above. There was no toilet or bathroom, and on the first day I went there I saw a snake.

![Image 16](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Hien-02-1024x806.jpg)

_The house where Hien and her mother were living in 2004._

And yet, Hien was going to school every day, dressed in her uniform looking cheerful and studious.

It wasn’t that she was unaffected by her difficult home life. It was that she had learned to hide her fear, to hold it down, and just get on with things.

Blue Dragon was tiny at that time – we had no resources or staff, just a drive to help kids.

Seeing Hien’s appalling living conditions, we knew we had to do something.

Something big.

### Taking action

You can [read the whole story here](http://www.bluedragon.org/stories/the-house-freed-her), including an update of where Hien is today.

But in short, what we did was: everything.

Everything that Hien needed.

We found someone to donate land to her family, that is now hers forever.

Then we built a house. It is no mansion, but it was big enough for mother and daughter, well constructed, and included a private bathroom – the first time in her life Hien had had one.

![Image 17](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Hien-03-768x1024.jpg)

_The house we built for Hien._

While we did this, we started assisting Hien with her studies. Her mother was unwell and had no stable income, so we relieved her of the burden of paying Hien’s school fees.

Once Hien completed Grade 12, we gave her a scholarship to university. Even after that, we helped her secure an opportunity to study abroad.

Hien now has a great job and family of her own. Her son has had a very different childhood to his mother’s; he could not imagine the hardship that she once endured. And that’s exactly as it should be.

The intergenerational poverty cycle has been broken.

### A big idea

At Blue Dragon, we call this a “massive intervention.”

When we meet a child living in hardship or crisis, we don’t look for the quick-fix solution. We don’t just deal with the most obvious problem.

Instead, we look at what it will take to make a lasting change. To really make a powerful difference.

This means we don’t always choose the cheapest or simplest option. And it also means making a long-term commitment to each child.

It takes a significant effort and it’s worth it.

Our experience of helping Hien taught us that interventions to keep kids safe had to be “massive.”

And we still do that today.

Every rescue of a trafficked person is a massive step of an even larger intervention to change someone’s life. It’s how we have had so much success over the years of working with kids in the toughest of circumstances and transforming their future.

That Hien now leads a happy, independent life free from the fear and shame of poverty is a testament to Blue Dragon’s “massive intervention.”

May there be many more to come.

Typhoon Yagi seems like ancient history now.

Without a doubt, there will be more next week, too.

Which is exactly what has been happening here in Vietnam. It’s a very long road ahead, because the damage has been tremendous and widespread.

However: it has begun.

Blue Dragon and an army of volunteers have been assisting with the cleanup. Removing fallen trees, cleaning mud out of shacks and replacing lost belongings.

## [When it rains](https://lifeisalongstory.com/when-it-rains/)

A massive storm hit and quickly passed, leaving a trail of devastation. But as the calm settled in, the real destruction began.

It was meant to be a week of celebration.

Around the world, [over 1,000 people took part in the Blue Dragon Walk](https://lifeisalongstory.com/the-day-of-the-walk/). But not in Hanoi, where a typhoon the day before damaged the park where our event was planned, or in other cities affected by the rain.

Despite the ferocity of Typhoon Yagi, it seemed that its impact was limited.

![Image 25](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Hanoi-park-1024x683.jpg)

_A Hanoi park immediately after the typhoon._

In coastal areas of Vietnam, there was serious damage to property. But once the storm had passed, everyone was hopeful we could quickly repair and move on.

We were wrong.

The extent of Yagi and the heaviness of the rain meant that whole provinces of northern Vietnam were saturated.

Within two days, rivers started to rise well above their normal levels. And then landslides started in the mountains.

From being relieved in a moment of calm, Vietnam went into full disaster mode.

As of writing this blog, over 260 people have died and scores more are missing.

Tens of thousands have lost their homes. By far, most are people already living in poverty.

Houses totally swamped by rivers or crushed by dirt.

![Image 26](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Northern-house-1024x768.jpg)

_A house in the northern mountains, devastated by a landslide._

One village was completely wiped out by a landslide, killing 46 people.

Bridges and roads have been washed away.

At one point, Blue Dragon had to evacuate our Hanoi building, which serves as both our children’s centre and our organisational headquarters, because of fear of flooding.

![Image 27](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Delivering-supplies-in-Hanoi-1024x768.jpg)

_Delivering supplies to families while the flood waters are still high._

There’s an old saying: _When it rains, it pours._

Usually we say this with pessimism. When something goes wrong, it goes wrong in a big way.

And Yagi is a good example of that.

![Image 28](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Disaster-zone-1024x682.jpg)

_Homes in the aftermath of flooding._

But the opposite also holds true. When things go well, they go well in a big way.

The response to this catastrophe is an outpouring of love and practical assistance.

Around the globe, people have been donating to Blue Dragon and to other great charities as well. The response has been rapid and many donations come in with a message of care and support.

People, schools and companies in Hanoi have been turning up to Blue Dragon with truck loads of supplies: food, water, clothing. All of it is going straight out to people who need it.

![Image 29](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Supplies-1024x575.jpg)

_Getting supplies to a family._

And on the ground, community members have been pitching in to help clean up as soon as it was safe.

Over the weekend, groups of both Vietnamese people and expatriates rose up and went out cleaning up the city.

Armies of student volunteers have traveled to locations where they’re needed most.

![Image 30](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/The-cleanup-begins-768x1024.jpg)

_The cleanup begins._

Everyone is doing their bit.

This is not to say that there’s a silver lining. There’s not. This is a terrible time and the hurt among so many people is still very raw.

But in the darkness, we still see the goodness of humanity. And that’s what keeps us going.

## [One thing that never changes](https://lifeisalongstory.com/one-thing-that-never-changes/)

Human trafficking is arguably one of the most agile ‘businesses’ in our world. How can we hope to disrupt a crime that is constantly changing?

Ngoc is the first child we rescued from human trafficking.

Aged 13, he had been taken from his sea-side village to sprawling Ho Chi Minh City, where he was forced to sell flowers to tourists for 12 or more hours a day.

When we investigated, we found that hundreds of children from his central Vietnamese community had been trafficked. Like Ngoc, some were selling flowers on the streets. Most were in garment factories, toiling away for no pay in terrible conditions.

Chi was the first person we [rescued from a brothel in China](https://lifeisalongstory.com/rescue/). She had been trafficked and sold at age 17 by someone she thought was her boyfriend.

When we went to find her, we released 6 other girls and young women who were also enslaved. We’ve been working on cross-border human trafficking in the years since.

But those initial forms of trafficking we dealt with no longer exist in any substantial form.

### Shifting sands

Village children are no longer being trafficked to factories and to sell flowers. Blue Dragon worked with the community for 12 years on this issue before it reached an end. It’s now a relic of history.

Nor are Vietnamese girls being trafficked into Chinese brothels as they were. What was once a serious issue is now a rare phenomenon. This is largely thanks to efforts by Chinese authorities to crack down on brothels.

The issues that once fully occupied our radar are now occasional blips on the screen.

However, that’s not to say that human trafficking has ended. Instead, it’s morphed – several times over.

In each new iteration, it takes on new characteristics and new forms of brutality. Today, the main form of slavery we are dealing with is the trafficking of Vietnamese people to Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos for forced online scamming.

Just a few years ago, this was unheard of.

And what is now a significant crisis, with an estimated 300,000 people enslaved and forced to scam money from people online, will one day be an awful memory.

Online scamming will certainly continue, but AI is likely to replace the need for large numbers of people to be forced to work online day and night.

And as the pressure on governments to take action against organised scamming continues to grow, the traffickers are already looking at alternative business models.

### The next wave?

In northern Myanmar, there are indications that some of the gangs running the scam compounds are turning their attention to cannabis production for the Thai market.

![Image 50](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/greenhouse-1024x472.jpeg)

_A greenhouse being built for cannabis production in Myanmar._

If this happens, they’ll be looking for slave labour for not only the growing, but also the processing and packaging of their product to give themselves a competitive advantage in the marketplace.

Is this to be the next major iteration of human trafficking in Southeast Asia? It might be. Or it could be something else that’s yet to surface.

Because the one thing that’s absolutely certain with human trafficking is that it will continue to change. The specific types of slavery we see today will end, or at least reduce substantially.

And something else will rise to take their place.

That’s why there’s no single ‘fix’ for human trafficking. No silver bullet.

### The answer: Agility

Blue Dragon’s interventions range from prevention programs to rescue… and then to the care of people after they have been set free. Over time, all of this is needed.

Specifically where and how we do these things will keep changing. So we must be agile enough to keep changing along with them. And that change has to be quick.

We’ve built agility into our organisational structure and our mindset. When a new issue emerges, or even a global crisis like Covid, we’re able to pivot to meet the challenge.

This gives us confidence that we can really make a difference.

Because if some forms of trafficking can be ended, then they all can.

## [Dreaming beyond survival](https://lifeisalongstory.com/dreaming-beyond-survival/)

How can kids who grow up in slavery or on the streets transform into thriving adults with bright futures?

[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Flifeisalongstory.com "Facebook")[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Life%20is%20a%20long%20story%20-%20Finding%20hope%20in%20unlikely%20places%3A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20A%20blog%20by%20%20the%20founder%20of%20Blue%20Dragon%20Children%27s%20Foundation%20in%20Vietnam.&url=https%3A%2F%2Flifeisalongstory.com "Twitter")[](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https%3A%2F%2Flifeisalongstory.com "Linkedin")[](https://api.whatsapp.com/send?text=Life%20is%20a%20long%20story%20-%20Finding%20hope%20in%20unlikely%20places%3A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20A%20blog%20by%20%20the%20founder%20of%20Blue%20Dragon%20Children%27s%20Foundation%20in%20Vietnam.%20https%3A%2F%2Flifeisalongstory.com "Whatsapp")[](https://lifeisalongstory.com/ "Email")

The news from Blue Dragon last week was of both triumph and heartbreak.

After weeks of nail-biting planning and preparing, several rescue operations came to completion.

Most of the people we rescued had been enslaved in forced online scamming. These are compounds in Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos where people are forced, under threat of beatings and torture, to trick people out of their life savings using fake websites, phone messages and social media.

One of our rescues involved bringing home a 17-year-old girl from a brothel in Myanmar. She was held captive there for three years.

You can imagine the horrors she has been through.

Once each person is safe, Blue Dragon has lawyers to represent them, psychologists to provide trauma counseling and social workers to help them start over.

And while these operations were taking place, something equally transformative—but vastly different—was happening elsewhere.

### Field trip

Thirteen kids from Blue Dragon traveled to Singapore to spend the week on a cultural and educational exchange. They were accompanied by staff and some of our alumni who went to support them.

The teens visited tourist sites, stayed in wonderful accommodation (thank you, Holiday Inn Express Suites Novena!), and spent time in the homes of families who live in Singapore.

The trip was funded by United World College SEA, whose students and teachers worked for a year to raise this money.

![Image 2](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Singapore-1-1024x768.jpg)

_Blue Dragon kids in Singapore preparing their performance._

For all of the kids, this was their first time traveling abroad, staying in hotels, or even imagining a life outside Vietnam.

Seeing their awe at Singapore’s bustling streets and performing in front of an audience was a reminder of how far they’ve come—and how much potential lies within them.

Apart from having a great time, the Blue Dragon kids and the United World College students worked together to put on a grand performance at the end of the week.

### Different worlds?

Moving from life-and-death rescue operations to cultural experiences in another country might seem worlds apart.

But Blue Dragon wants kids to hope for more than mere _survival_.

When we get kids off the street, or bring them home from slavery, we want them to have the world at their feet.

To have dreams and see what’s possible beyond their own horizon.

To live a life that they love, not one that’s simply free of extreme hardship.

We’ve been fortunate to have the chance to take kids to Singapore for some years. So we’ve seen the impact that experiences like these have on young people as they grow up.

What we find is that kids who are exposed to new possibilities are much more likely to pursue an education and a career.

Some even go on to study abroad, and many end up in jobs they would never have thought possible just a few years earlier.

These different parts of our work aren’t worlds apart at all. They’re simply different points on the spectrum of ending disadvantage and transforming lives.

The 13 kids have returned to Vietnam, exhausted from an intense week and buzzing with delight.

Their eyes have been opened to something they never imagined. They’ve made new friends and performed in public.

And most importantly: They’ve shown themselves that they are more than ‘survivors’.

They were offered a chance to shine. They took the opportunity. And they succeeded.

## [Worthless things](https://lifeisalongstory.com/worthless-things/)

Changing lives is neither a science nor an art. It takes care and commitment, sometimes over months or years. And it’s all built on one crucial but elusive foundation.

This week, I spoke on two webinars about Blue Dragon’s 20-year journey.

We started out as a handful of volunteers teaching English to street kids in Hanoi.

Today we’re working around Vietnam preventing human trafficking. We’ve led law reform initiatives, put thousands of children through school, and have rescued almost 1,700 people from slavery. So far!

During a webinar, someone asked: In our work, how do we build trust with the kids we’re helping?

An excellent question, because trust isn’t assumed. Blue Dragon’s 20 years of experience means nothing to a child we meet sleeping under a bridge, or a teenage girl locked into a brothel.

The people we meet in these crisis situations have been abused and neglected. They might not trust _anyone_, let alone a stranger from an organisation they’ve never encountered.

But we can’t help if the person doesn’t trust us. So how do we do it?

### Playing games

Back when we were starting up as a charity, we had a handful of brilliant supporters… as well as plenty of critics.

Some people assumed our work either wasn’t important or wouldn’t last long. That we’d soon discover how difficult the work was and give up.

As we continued to grow and become established, I remember one person, vastly more experienced than me, telling me that Blue Dragon’s work was useless. (To her credit, she told me this to my face).

We were doing “worthless things,” she told me. Just playing games with kids. There was no real benefit to our work.

### No strings attached

One of Blue Dragon’s key activities at that time – and still today – was weekend football for street kids.

And yes, a lot of our effort went into social activities like a drumming circle and art classes.

![Image 4](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Skye-at-drumming-1024x674.jpg)

_Skye Maconachie leading a drumming circle for street kids in 2004._  
_Today, she’s a co-CEO of the organisation._

Much of our time was spent simply getting to know kids, meeting with them, listening to them. We did all of this with no expectation or obligation.

It was up to the kids to decide whether they wanted to go back to school or continue on the streets and our care for them had no strings attached.

The purpose of all these “worthless things”? We were building trust.

Today, as we reach thousands of children and families around the country, we continue to work by the same principle.

Trust must come first and it must be earned.

Whether it’s the rescue of someone from slavery or meeting a child on the street, the decision to receive our help is theirs.

For them to make that decision, they need to know us. Not our web profile or what awards we’ve won. They need to know our character. Our heart.

### Down in the dirt

That’s why Blue Dragon staff can be found sitting by the side of the road chatting to a family. Or taking a group of kids to play games and have a meal.

![Image 5](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Street-outreach-1024x768.jpg)

_Blue Dragon street outreach workers running activities with homeless children._

It’s why our anti-trafficking initiatives in rural areas typically begin by helping communities to meet the needs that _they_ identify: a bridge to cross a stream, or a water filter system for the local school.

All of these activities meet a local need and _at the same time_ build trust with people and communities.

![Image 6](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/solar-lights-1024x458.jpg)

_Installing solar lights in a mountain village._

That trust gives us the stepping stones to then make sustainable, transformative change.

When kids know they can trust us, we can help them rebuild family connections and get back to school.

When communities see that we really do have their best interests at heart, they will work with us to keep human traffickers out of their village.

It all begins with trust.

And nothing could be more valuable.

_[Blue Dragon Child](http://www.bluedragon.org/)[r](http://www.bluedragon.org/)[en’s Foundation](http://www.bluedragon.org/)is on a mission to end human trafficking._

![Image 7](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/5872a03f1417206d1d72d3fa455decaf42f47656f4b4418313dd1d96352a9174?s=49&d=mm&r=g)Author [Michael Brosowski](https://lifeisalongstory.com/author/michael/)Posted on [November 10, 2024 November 9, 2024](https://lifeisalongstory.com/worthless-things/)[Leave a comment on Worthless things](https://lifeisalongstory.com/worthless-things/#respond)
## [Surviving the impossible](https://lifeisalongstory.com/surviving-the-impossible/)

When a simple search for work turns into a nightmare, lives are shattered in ways few can imagine. Thuy and Tuan’s stories show the brutal realities of slavery and the courage it takes to survive.

### _Thuy’s story_

When she crossed the border back to Vietnam, Thuy’s first words were: “I never thought I’d survive.”

She ventured out from home at age 28, leaving her 3-year-old son in the care of her mother and extended family.

All she wanted was the dignity of a job. To earn money for her child and parents. To have a better life.

But Thuy was tricked by people online who had gained her trust.

Instead of securing a job in a restaurant, she was trafficked to Myanmar and sold to a brothel.

The many months that she was enslaved there are a story too terrifying to tell. Trapped in a war zone, separated from her family and used as a disposable object, Thuy was sure she would die before she could ever get home.

It was almost two years before Thuy found a way to call for help. Blue Dragon organised a rescue operation and brought her home.

Even though she was free from her captors, the journey from northern Myanmar to Vietnam was frightening and tense.

Only her hope of seeing her son kept her going. And now they are back together.

![Image 8](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Thuy-and-her-son-reunited-2-768x1024.jpeg)

_Thuy and her son, reunited after almost two years apart._

### _Tuan’s story_

Tuan was deceived with similar tactics: an online connection that seemed completely authentic.

Until the moment he was overcome with force and locked into a compound.

Tuan traveled to Cambodia in search of work.

He did his research beforehand, talking to friends and scouring the internet. He believed he knew the risks and was confident no harm would come to him.

So when he realised he had been tricked and was being forced to work in captivity, his initial reaction was to demand his freedom.

Tuan was beaten and tortured into submission, then put to work in an online scamming operation. It was more than a year before he could get word to Blue Dragon, who got him out and back to his family within a few weeks.

![Image 9](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Tuan-crossing-the-border-768x1024.jpeg)

_Tuan crossing the border._

### _The chapters to come_

Even though I’ve been involved in rescue operations like these for many years, I still can’t comprehend the trauma that Thuy and Tuan are living with now.

Both put their trust in others. They went in search of employment, believing they were doing the right thing.

Their choice to leave home and travel for work was not easy and their decision was not made lightly.

So the betrayal that they experienced, and then the violence they endured month after month, left them feeling helpless and weak. And guilty.

Neither Thuy nor Tuan did anything wrong. But one of the great tricks of human traffickers is to make their victims feel like it was their own fault.

On top of the physical pain of torture and the loss of freedom, they live now with doubts about their self worth. And the question that will always haunt them: Why did this happen to them?

The toll of human trafficking is a lifetime of regret, guilt and pain.

Thuy and Tuan have a chance to start over but will need help for many months and years to come.

They were fortunate, in one sense, to be rescued: hundreds of thousands of people just like them are enslaved around Southeast Asia in brothels and scamming compounds, as they were, with no way out.

But they will carry these scars for many years to come.

## [Always more to the story](https://lifeisalongstory.com/always-more-to-the-story/)

There’s an anniversary that Bi never forgets: the day that changed his life forever. But he knows that his story is far from over.

Sipping our coffee by the lake, Bi looked over to me and said:

“November 8. It will be 6 years.”

I knew what he was referring to, because in years passed he’s mentioned this anniversary.

This is the date that, in 2018, he first encountered Blue Dragon.

It was such an important milestone in Bi’s life that he acknowledges it with every passing year.

He was still a child then. He had left his home in the village to come to the city, looking for an escape.

Life at home was hard.

His relationship with his father was fractured beyond repair. So after trying over and over, Bi eventually gave up.

Surely he could make it on the city streets alone. It couldn’t be worse than home, could it?

But it was. The streets are no place for kids to survive; not in any city, any country.

And so finding Blue Dragon was the turning point he needed.

### Fine young man

Sitting across from me now, Bi is still the same smiling, optimistic person he was when I first met him.

What’s changed is that he’s vastly more confident now. He carries himself with calm purpose; kindness beams from his smile.

Bi is in his final years of high school. Even though he’s in his early 20s, he’s enrolled in a class and is working hard at his studies. When he graduates, he plans to apply for university and earn a degree in social work.

A few nights each week, he helps out at the Blue Dragon emergency shelter. Bi works alongside staff to care for kids who we’ve just met out on the streets – kids like he once was.

![Image 11](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Bi-and-a-street-kid-927x1024.jpg)

_Bi walking with a street kid_.

But this journey of 6 years has not followed a straight line.

### The winding road

In fact, Bi’s story has had more ups and downs, more surprises along the way, than many of the young people we meet.

Over the years, there have been times when he enrolled in school… and then stopped going.

At times he’s been out sleeping rough on the streets again. For a while he returned to his village, hoping to repair his relationship with his family. When he ended up living alone in a house without electricity, he came back under the wing of Blue Dragon. And for a while he was working as a ‘shipper’, carrying goods around the city on his motorbike.

Finishing his coffee, Bi tells me that he’s not worried about the future any more. He has a plan and for the first time in his memory, he’s stable.

Above all, he’s grateful that for 6 years he’s had Blue Dragon in his life… through all the ups and downs.

And while Bi’s future is undoubtedly bright, he and I both know that there will be more to his story. More surprises, more changes along the way.

Because life is like that. It really is a long story.

And that’s OK. Bi is mature enough now to know that he doesn’t need to see the future in order to accept it.

He just needs to give it his best and to know that someone will always be there by his side.

## [It’s all in the moments](https://lifeisalongstory.com/its-all-in-the-moments/)

A girl who survives on the streets. A boy who refuses the care that he needs. What does it take to turn their lives around?

Ngoc celebrated her first birthday this week.

She turned 15.

Growing up on the streets of Ho Chi Minh City, there’s not much joy in Ngoc’s life.

Her days are about survival. That means hanging with a group of friends who can protect her and moving about the city to places she feels safe.

Ngoc has a grandmother and younger siblings. She cares for them very much. But things never seem to work out when she’s with them, so she escapes to the streets where she feels that she belongs.

Blue Dragon has been getting to know Ngoc and her friends but it takes time to build trust.

We wish we could get her back to her family right away. We wish we could heal the years of damaged relationships around her and restore the childhood that she’s lost.

And while we’d like to move fast, we know that we have to move at Ngoc’s pace.

All this will happen when she’s ready.

So day by day, we do what we can to make her life whole.

### Celebration

Friday was the first time she’s ever celebrated her own birthday.

When we learned that she had a birthday coming, we saw an opportunity to create a moment of joy.

![Image 13](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Ngocs-birthday-1024x767.jpg)

_Ngoc, 15, cutting her first birthday cake._

We bought a cake and set up in a cafe where Ngoc could invite her friends to celebrate with her.

Everyone sang happy birthday and enjoyed the sweet cake, completely forgetting the hardships of their lives.

Later, Ngoc messaged the Blue Dragon social worker to say with pride that she was so happy and had taken the remaining cake home for her siblings and her grandmother to enjoy.

I’m sure she’ll never forget that first birthday celebration.

### A crack in the armour

In Hanoi, meantime, we’ve been caring for a teen boy named Hoan.

He’s from a town 4 hours south of the city and has been on the streets for a couple of years now.

Like Ngoc, he has a family that he cares for but just can’t live with. He works at night in the tourist district of Hanoi, making enough money to get from day to day.

He enjoys meeting with Blue Dragon staff and loves going for a milk tea or a bowl of phở. But he’s wary of receiving help, guarding his independence above everything.

Two weeks ago, Hoan perforated his eardrum. It’s caused him terrible pain.

In fact, it’s been so bad that he finally accepted some help. We’ve been taking him to the hospital to treat his ear and making sure he has enough to eat while he can’t work.

His eardrum is starting to heal now. Another trip to the hospital on Saturday confirmed that he’s on the mend.

![Image 14](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Hoan-at-the-hospital-782x1024.jpg)

_Hoan at the hospital._

And after the checkup: a bowl of phở and shopping for new clothes.

Hoan beamed with joy as he chose a couple of simple t-shirts.

This tough young guy who has learned to survive on the city streets transformed into a cheerful little boy. He looked like a child on Christmas morning.

### Transformative moments

Blue Dragon’s work is about so much more than buying birthday cakes and t-shirts.

But somehow, these moments are _exactly_ what we’re about.

We all dream of changing the world. Making it a better place for those who are poor and suffering.

And much of what Blue Dragon does is focused on systemic change to end human trafficking and keep kids safe.

From day to day, though, change is incremental. Step by step.

There’s no wave of the wand, no granting of a wish to make everything better.

Instead, it starts with buying a birthday cake for a girl who’s never had one before. And taking a boy for an ear check and some shopping.

Creating those moments of joy is where change begins.

_[Blue Dragon Child](http://www.bluedragon.org/)[r](http://www.bluedragon.org/)[en’s Foundation](http://www.bluedragon.org/)is on a mission to end human trafficking._

![Image 15](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/5872a03f1417206d1d72d3fa455decaf42f47656f4b4418313dd1d96352a9174?s=49&d=mm&r=g)Author [Michael Brosowski](https://lifeisalongstory.com/author/michael/)Posted on [October 13, 2024 October 13, 2024](https://lifeisalongstory.com/its-all-in-the-moments/)[3 Comments on It’s all in the moments](https://lifeisalongstory.com/its-all-in-the-moments/#comments)
## [Massive interventions](https://lifeisalongstory.com/massive-interventions/)

Hien went to school each day and put in her best effort with a smile. But deep inside she carried fear and shame. She could see no way out.

Because it’s Blue Dragon’s 20th birthday, we’ve been looking back at kids we helped long ago and writing stories about where they are now.

This week, we shared [Hien’s story](https://www.bluedragon.org/stories/the-house-freed-her/).

We didn’t know it at the time, but Hien played an important role in shaping Blue Dragon in our early days.

### Hien’s story

I met her 20 years ago, when she was living with her mother in a truly decrepit house.

The roof had holes large enough to see the sky above. There was no toilet or bathroom, and on the first day I went there I saw a snake.

![Image 16](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Hien-02-1024x806.jpg)

_The house where Hien and her mother were living in 2004._

And yet, Hien was going to school every day, dressed in her uniform looking cheerful and studious.

It wasn’t that she was unaffected by her difficult home life. It was that she had learned to hide her fear, to hold it down, and just get on with things.

Blue Dragon was tiny at that time – we had no resources or staff, just a drive to help kids.

Seeing Hien’s appalling living conditions, we knew we had to do something.

Something big.

### Taking action

You can [read the whole story here](http://www.bluedragon.org/stories/the-house-freed-her), including an update of where Hien is today.

But in short, what we did was: everything.

Everything that Hien needed.

We found someone to donate land to her family, that is now hers forever.

Then we built a house. It is no mansion, but it was big enough for mother and daughter, well constructed, and included a private bathroom – the first time in her life Hien had had one.

![Image 17](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Hien-03-768x1024.jpg)

_The house we built for Hien._

While we did this, we started assisting Hien with her studies. Her mother was unwell and had no stable income, so we relieved her of the burden of paying Hien’s school fees.

Once Hien completed Grade 12, we gave her a scholarship to university. Even after that, we helped her secure an opportunity to study abroad.

Hien now has a great job and family of her own. Her son has had a very different childhood to his mother’s; he could not imagine the hardship that she once endured. And that’s exactly as it should be.

The intergenerational poverty cycle has been broken.

### A big idea

At Blue Dragon, we call this a “massive intervention.”

When we meet a child living in hardship or crisis, we don’t look for the quick-fix solution. We don’t just deal with the most obvious problem.

Instead, we look at what it will take to make a lasting change. To really make a powerful difference.

This means we don’t always choose the cheapest or simplest option. And it also means making a long-term commitment to each child.

It takes a significant effort and it’s worth it.

Our experience of helping Hien taught us that interventions to keep kids safe had to be “massive.”

And we still do that today.

Every rescue of a trafficked person is a massive step of an even larger intervention to change someone’s life. It’s how we have had so much success over the years of working with kids in the toughest of circumstances and transforming their future.

That Hien now leads a happy, independent life free from the fear and shame of poverty is a testament to Blue Dragon’s “massive intervention.”

May there be many more to come.

_[Blue Dragon Child](http://www.bluedragon.org/)[r](http://www.bluedragon.org/)[en’s Foundation](http://www.bluedragon.org/)is on a mission to end human trafficking._

![Image 18](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/5872a03f1417206d1d72d3fa455decaf42f47656f4b4418313dd1d96352a9174?s=49&d=mm&r=g)Author [Michael Brosowski](https://lifeisalongstory.com/author/michael/)Posted on [October 6, 2024 October 5, 2024](https://lifeisalongstory.com/massive-interventions/)[Leave a comment on Massive interventions](https://lifeisalongstory.com/massive-interventions/#respond)
## [And now the cleanup](https://lifeisalongstory.com/and-now-the-cleanup/)

The storm is long gone, but those who lost their homes and belongings have an even longer road ahead.

Typhoon Yagi seems like ancient history now.

Two weeks on and their are new crises around the globe to grab the headlines.

Without a doubt, there will be more next week, too.

But as the headlines move on, those affected are left to clean up, rebuild, and start again.

Which is exactly what has been happening here in Vietnam. It’s a very long road ahead, because the damage has been tremendous and widespread.

![Image 19](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/c58ef5df-c3e6-4c3f-88c8-58a6280c1bfb-1024x462.jpeg)

_A riverside community devastated by flooding._

![Image 20](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Northern-house-1-1024x768.jpg)

_A house in a northern H’mong village hit by a landslide._

However: it has begun.

Blue Dragon and an army of volunteers have been assisting with the cleanup. Removing fallen trees, cleaning mud out of shacks and replacing lost belongings.

![Image 21](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Xin-Cai-4-1024x768.jpg)

_Relocating a family to a neighbour’s home after a landslide destroyed their traditional timber house._

![Image 22](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Volunteers-1024x768.jpg)

_Volunteers pitching in together for the cleanup._

For me, there is one picture that most sums up Blue Dragon’s response to Yagi.

One of our social workers out in the community checking in with families. Down on her knees in a flooded street so that the child she’s talking to can look at her eye-to-eye.

![Image 23](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/social-worker-1024x768.jpg)

_Blue Dragon social worker checking in with a child._

This is our response: from the heart, human to human. Respectful and equal.

The cleaning and rebuilding will continue for many months. And it’s all possible because people around the world have donated, or put their hand up to volunteer, right at the time help was needed most.

To all who have been a part of this: Thank you.

[_Blue Dragon is still able to accept donations to help victims of Typhoon Yagi. All help will go to the effort to rebuild homes and livelihoods in northern Vietnam._](https://www.bluedragon.org/emergency-appeal-yagi/)

![Image 24](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/5872a03f1417206d1d72d3fa455decaf42f47656f4b4418313dd1d96352a9174?s=49&d=mm&r=g)Author [Michael Brosowski](https://lifeisalongstory.com/author/michael/)Posted on [September 23, 2024 September 23, 2024](https://lifeisalongstory.com/and-now-the-cleanup/)[Leave a comment on And now the cleanup](https://lifeisalongstory.com/and-now-the-cleanup/#respond)
## [When it rains](https://lifeisalongstory.com/when-it-rains/)

A massive storm hit and quickly passed, leaving a trail of devastation. But as the calm settled in, the real destruction began.

It was meant to be a week of celebration.

Around the world, [over 1,000 people took part in the Blue Dragon Walk](https://lifeisalongstory.com/the-day-of-the-walk/). But not in Hanoi, where a typhoon the day before damaged the park where our event was planned, or in other cities affected by the rain.

Despite the ferocity of Typhoon Yagi, it seemed that its impact was limited.

![Image 25](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Hanoi-park-1024x683.jpg)

_A Hanoi park immediately after the typhoon._

In coastal areas of Vietnam, there was serious damage to property. But once the storm had passed, everyone was hopeful we could quickly repair and move on.

We were wrong.

The extent of Yagi and the heaviness of the rain meant that whole provinces of northern Vietnam were saturated.

Within two days, rivers started to rise well above their normal levels. And then landslides started in the mountains.

From being relieved in a moment of calm, Vietnam went into full disaster mode.

As of writing this blog, over 260 people have died and scores more are missing.

Tens of thousands have lost their homes. By far, most are people already living in poverty.

Houses totally swamped by rivers or crushed by dirt.

![Image 26](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Northern-house-1024x768.jpg)

_A house in the northern mountains, devastated by a landslide._

One village was completely wiped out by a landslide, killing 46 people.

Bridges and roads have been washed away.

At one point, Blue Dragon had to evacuate our Hanoi building, which serves as both our children’s centre and our organisational headquarters, because of fear of flooding.

![Image 27](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Delivering-supplies-in-Hanoi-1024x768.jpg)

_Delivering supplies to families while the flood waters are still high._

There’s an old saying: _When it rains, it pours._

Usually we say this with pessimism. When something goes wrong, it goes wrong in a big way.

And Yagi is a good example of that.

![Image 28](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Disaster-zone-1024x682.jpg)

_Homes in the aftermath of flooding._

But the opposite also holds true. When things go well, they go well in a big way.

The response to this catastrophe is an outpouring of love and practical assistance.

Around the globe, people have been donating to Blue Dragon and to other great charities as well. The response has been rapid and many donations come in with a message of care and support.

People, schools and companies in Hanoi have been turning up to Blue Dragon with truck loads of supplies: food, water, clothing. All of it is going straight out to people who need it.

![Image 29](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Supplies-1024x575.jpg)

_Getting supplies to a family._

And on the ground, community members have been pitching in to help clean up as soon as it was safe.

Over the weekend, groups of both Vietnamese people and expatriates rose up and went out cleaning up the city.

Armies of student volunteers have traveled to locations where they’re needed most.

![Image 30](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/The-cleanup-begins-768x1024.jpg)

_The cleanup begins._

Everyone is doing their bit.

This is not to say that there’s a silver lining. There’s not. This is a terrible time and the hurt among so many people is still very raw.

But in the darkness, we still see the goodness of humanity. And that’s what keeps us going.

## [The Day of the Walk](https://lifeisalongstory.com/the-day-of-the-walk/)

It’s been another big one.

The annual Blue Dragon Walk has taken place around the world.

I’m writing this week from Melbourne, where I joined the Walk along the Bay.

The day started sunny and bright, but for a while our Walkers were drenched with a classic Melbourne downpour. Yet they continued – and continued to smile!

Around the world, Walkers appeared everywhere.

![Image 32](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Toronto-768x1024.jpg)

_Toronto, Canada: The staff of Intrepid Travel organised a walk through the city._

![Image 33](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/7605c9e0-907e-4c59-a401-00755d2d26a2-1024x770.jpeg)

_Ho Chi Minh City: Blue Dragon’s newly formed staff team in the city did their bit!_

![Image 34](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Oxford-UK-1-768x1024.jpg)

_Oxford, UK._

![Image 35](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Bangkok-1024x768.jpg)

_Bangkok, Thailand: Yaana Ventures organised a great day for staff and guests._

![Image 36](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Oslo-Norway-768x1024.jpg)

_Oslo, Norway._

![Image 37](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Hoi-AN-1024x768.jpg)

_Hoi An, Vietnam: The team of Chops, a much loved burger chain, arranged a Walk in the ancient city._

![Image 38](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Switzerland-574x1024.jpg)

_Lausanne, Switzerland: A marathon walk through mountains and villages._

![Image 39](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/458407182_1289441098706387_8718273182651233688_n-1024x768.jpg)

_Sydney, Australia: That background says it all!_

![Image 40](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/458933800_2267131200320897_4402693090033138910_n-768x1024.jpg)

_Chiang Mai, Thailand: To escape the heat, this team walked at night._

![Image 41](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Phu-Quoc-Isand.jpg)

_Phu Quoc Island, Vietnam: These Walkers from Accor Hotels were just one part of the hospitality chain’s broader participation in the day._

![Image 42](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Manchester-UK.jpg)

_Manchester, UK_.

![Image 43](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Sydney-again.jpg)

_Sydney again!_

![Image 44](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Singapore-1024x768.jpg)

_Singapore._

And many, many more. Too many for me to share in a single blog!

It’s a powerful statement to have so many people in so many places showing their support for the work of Blue Dragon.

A HUGE thank you to everyone who took part, including…

![Image 45](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Carasa-738x1024.jpg)![Image 46](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/458943008_8484364484964514_774296970616399085_n-768x1024.jpg)
… quite a few furry friends.

But there was one place where not many people walked.

![Image 47](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Hanoi-768x1024.jpg)

_Typhoon damage in Hanoi_.

Typhoon Yagi hit northern Vietnam hard over the weekend. The Blue Dragon Walk in Hanoi has been postponed until next weekend while the city cleans up.

![Image 48](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Yen-So-Park-2-1024x768.jpg)

_Cleaning up after the typhoon._

A few brave people did get out and walk in Hanoi, but there’s a lot of work to do before the city is back to normal.

Which means the Blue Dragon Walk is not over yet, but a lot of good has already been done.

As with everything Blue Dragon does, it’s only possible because of the incredible friends we have around the world.

The Walk is the result of a partnership with [Intrepid Travel](https://www.intrepidtravel.com/), who do all the behind-the-scenes work that’s needed for a global event like this.

Huge support from groups like [APT Travel](https://www.aptouring.com.au/), who offered matching donations and set up the Melbourne location, make a massive difference.

And then there’s Roll’d, who delivered platters of food for lunch at the Melbourne Walk… Accor, who had 22 hotels take part… and so many more.

I don’t want to sound like an advertorial, but many people deserve acknowledgement for their help.

Because this kind of community event is critical to Blue Dragon’s work.

And importantly, it gives people from all walks of life a chance to do their part to end human trafficking.

So to all who have taken part, donated, organised and helped:

Thank you.

_It’s not too late to get involved! You’re welcome [to sponsor my Walk here on the website](https://www.bluedragonwalk.org/michael-brosowski). Every dollar you donate goes to Blue Dragon’s work in Vietnam._

![Image 49](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/5872a03f1417206d1d72d3fa455decaf42f47656f4b4418313dd1d96352a9174?s=49&d=mm&r=g)Author [Michael Brosowski](https://lifeisalongstory.com/author/michael/)Posted on [September 9, 2024 September 9, 2024](https://lifeisalongstory.com/the-day-of-the-walk/)Tags [Fundraising event](https://lifeisalongstory.com/tag/fundraising-event/), [Human Trafficking](https://lifeisalongstory.com/tag/human-trafficking/)[Leave a comment on The Day of the Walk](https://lifeisalongstory.com/the-day-of-the-walk/#respond)
## [One thing that never changes](https://lifeisalongstory.com/one-thing-that-never-changes/)

Human trafficking is arguably one of the most agile ‘businesses’ in our world. How can we hope to disrupt a crime that is constantly changing?

Ngoc is the first child we rescued from human trafficking.

Aged 13, he had been taken from his sea-side village to sprawling Ho Chi Minh City, where he was forced to sell flowers to tourists for 12 or more hours a day.

When we investigated, we found that hundreds of children from his central Vietnamese community had been trafficked. Like Ngoc, some were selling flowers on the streets. Most were in garment factories, toiling away for no pay in terrible conditions.

Chi was the first person we [rescued from a brothel in China](https://lifeisalongstory.com/rescue/). She had been trafficked and sold at age 17 by someone she thought was her boyfriend.

When we went to find her, we released 6 other girls and young women who were also enslaved. We’ve been working on cross-border human trafficking in the years since.

But those initial forms of trafficking we dealt with no longer exist in any substantial form.

### Shifting sands

Village children are no longer being trafficked to factories and to sell flowers. Blue Dragon worked with the community for 12 years on this issue before it reached an end. It’s now a relic of history.

Nor are Vietnamese girls being trafficked into Chinese brothels as they were. What was once a serious issue is now a rare phenomenon. This is largely thanks to efforts by Chinese authorities to crack down on brothels.

The issues that once fully occupied our radar are now occasional blips on the screen.

However, that’s not to say that human trafficking has ended. Instead, it’s morphed – several times over.

In each new iteration, it takes on new characteristics and new forms of brutality. Today, the main form of slavery we are dealing with is the trafficking of Vietnamese people to Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos for forced online scamming.

Just a few years ago, this was unheard of.

And what is now a significant crisis, with an estimated 300,000 people enslaved and forced to scam money from people online, will one day be an awful memory.

Online scamming will certainly continue, but AI is likely to replace the need for large numbers of people to be forced to work online day and night.

And as the pressure on governments to take action against organised scamming continues to grow, the traffickers are already looking at alternative business models.

### The next wave?

In northern Myanmar, there are indications that some of the gangs running the scam compounds are turning their attention to cannabis production for the Thai market.

![Image 50](https://lifeisalongstory.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/greenhouse-1024x472.jpeg)

_A greenhouse being built for cannabis production in Myanmar._

If this happens, they’ll be looking for slave labour for not only the growing, but also the processing and packaging of their product to give themselves a competitive advantage in the marketplace.

Is this to be the next major iteration of human trafficking in Southeast Asia? It might be. Or it could be something else that’s yet to surface.

Because the one thing that’s absolutely certain with human trafficking is that it will continue to change. The specific types of slavery we see today will end, or at least reduce substantially.

And something else will rise to take their place.

That’s why there’s no single ‘fix’ for human trafficking. No silver bullet.

### The answer: Agility

Blue Dragon’s interventions range from prevention programs to rescue… and then to the care of people after they have been set free. Over time, all of this is needed.

Specifically where and how we do these things will keep changing. So we must be agile enough to keep changing along with them. And that change has to be quick.

We’ve built agility into our organisational structure and our mindset. When a new issue emerges, or even a global crisis like Covid, we’re able to pivot to meet the challenge.

This gives us confidence that we can really make a difference.

Because if some forms of trafficking can be ended, then they all can.

_On Sunday September 8, the Blue Dragon Walk will be held around the world. Thank you to all who’ve registered to take part! It’s not too late for you to join – [sign up here](https://www.bluedragonwalk.org/). And if you’d rather sit the day out, [please consider sponsoring the Walk of our co-CEO Vi Do](https://www.bluedragonwalk.org/vi-do). Donations for his walk will be doubled by our friends at APT Travel_.

May 17, 2023, 1:44 PM UTC

By [Julianne McShane](https://www.nbcnews.com/author/julianne-mcshane-ncpn729621)

Ten teenage hikers who spent their Friday night lost on the trails of a Southern California canyon before a search and rescue team found them with the help of an iPhone feature "were not prepared" for their climb, officials said.

Members of the group — who are all 16 to 18 years old — spent about three hours Friday stuck on the trails of Santa Paula Canyon, in Los Padres National Forest, without proper hiking clothing, water and lighting equipment before they were rescued, Ventura County Sheriff’s Deputy Mackenzie Spears said in a text message.

"Most had t-shirts and shorts," Spears said. She added that temperatures were in the 60s and that "there were multiple water crossings and they needed to scramble" in certain sections of the hike, or climb steep terrain by hand.

Spears said in a news release that "most of the hikers were not prepared" and that the search and rescue team supplied them with food, water and equipment to light the trail on their way back.

The teens reached out to the sheriff's office around 8 p.m. Friday when they found themselves lost on the trails, the news release said.

The group made contact with emergency officials using Apple's emergency SOS feature, which allows iPhone users to call or text local emergency services, sometimes even without cell service or Wi-Fi access. The feature allowed them to share their possible location and conditions with emergency personnel, said the sheriff's office, which added that the teens' parents also reported them missing.

![Image 6: Group of missing teen hikers, found using iPhone feature, 'were not prepared' for climb, officials say.](https://media-cldnry.s-nbcnews.com/image/upload/t_fit-760w,f_avif,q_auto:best/rockcms/2023-05/230517-teen-hikers-mb-1335-884293.jpg)

Hikers are aided back to safety at Santa Paula Canyon, Calif., on Friday.Ventura County Sheriff's Office

More than a dozen members of the [Upper Ojai Search and Rescue](https://www.ojaisar.org/)[t](https://www.ojaisar.org/)[eam](https://www.ojaisar.org/), a group of local volunteers, headed out to look for the hikers within 30 minutes of having received their plea for help, the sheriff's office said.

After an approximately three-hour, 4-mile hike into the canyon that included "low visibility, multiple stream crossings and trails that had been previously damaged from the heavy rains," the rescue team found the missing teens on the so-called [Last Chance trail](https://www.hikingproject.com/trail/7031843/last-chance-trail) around 11:15 p.m., the sheriff's office said.

The hikers and the search and rescue team returned to the Santa Paula Canyon Trailhead around 2:40 a.m. Saturday, it said.

The search and rescue team [tweeted](https://twitter.com/OjaiSar/status/1658670056098889729?s=20) that the teens were the "biggest group we've rescued in a while." None required medical aid, the sheriff's office said.

The search and rescue team recommends that hikers and campers [alway](https://www.ojaisar.org/the-ten-essentials)[s](https://www.ojaisar.org/the-ten-essentials)[take e](https://www.ojaisar.org/the-ten-essentials)[s](https://www.ojaisar.org/the-ten-essentials)[s](https://www.ojaisar.org/the-ten-essentials)[entials](https://www.ojaisar.org/the-ten-essentials), including navigation, light sources, first aid supplies, food, water and a smartphone. [It also recommends](https://www.ojaisar.org/hiking-plan) that hikers fill out [hiking plan](https://www.ojaisar.org/hiking-plan)[s](https://www.ojaisar.org/hiking-plan) detailing where they plan to travel and what equipment they plan to take with them and leave them with someone not accompanying them in case of emergencies.

Over half of the 990 deaths in national parks from 2014 to 2016 —the most recent years for which data is available —were due to unintentional causes, [according to the National Park Service](https://www.nps.gov/orgs/1336/upload/CY14-CY16-Mortality-Dashboard-Key-Statistics.pdf). Drowning, motor vehicle crashes and falls were the leading causes of those deaths, it said.
